title: Tactical Combat Casualty Care (TCCC) Overview
summary: The three-phase TCCC framework and the MARCH order for treating serious injuries when help is delayed or the scene is still dangerous. Based on the current CoTCCC guidelines (May 2026) and civilian Stop the Bleed teaching.

steps.title: Know the three phases
steps.body: TCCC splits trauma care into three phases based on how dangerous the scene is. Care Under Fire (civilian version: Direct Threat Care) is while the threat is still active. Tactical Field Care (Indirect Threat Care) starts once you and the casualty are behind cover or the threat is gone. Tactical Evacuation Care is everything done while moving the casualty toward a hospital or clinic. The phase tells you how much you can safely do. In a grid-down setting the 'threat' may be fire, a collapsing building, traffic, floodwater, or an armed person. The rule is the same: a hurt rescuer helps no one, so control the danger before you treat.

steps.title: Care Under Fire - stop the threat, then the bleeding
steps.body: While the danger is active, the best medicine is getting everyone to safety. Move to cover and tell the casualty to move to cover and help themselves if able. If they cannot move, drag them. Pull people out of burning vehicles or buildings. The only treatment in this phase is a limb tourniquet for life-threatening arm or leg bleeding, placed quickly over the clothing, above the wound, if it is safe to do so. Do not try to manage the airway or look for small wounds yet. Those wait until you are safe.

steps.title: Tactical Field Care - start MARCH
steps.body: Once you are safe, make sure the area stays secure, sort casualties if there are several (see medical-014), and work through MARCH in order. M - Massive bleeding: find and stop any heavy bleeding with tourniquets, wound packing, or junctional pressure (medical-002, medical-003, medical-004). A - Airway: let a conscious person sit up and lean forward if that helps them breathe; roll an unconscious person into the recovery position (medical-007). R - Respiration: cover open chest wounds and watch for tension pneumothorax (medical-005). C - Circulation: check every tourniquet, look for shock (medical-006), and let trained medics start IV lines and fluids. H - Hypothermia prevention: get the casualty off the ground, remove wet clothing, and wrap them up. Bleeding comes before airway in trauma because heavy bleeding kills fastest.

steps.title: After MARCH - the rest of the list
steps.body: The current guidelines continue past MARCH. Watch for head injury signs (medical-020). Cover a penetrating eye injury with a rigid shield, not a pressure patch (medical-022). Keep checking breathing, pulse, and mental status. Treat pain - for a layperson that means over-the-counter medicine taken by the label, and never aspirin in a bleeding casualty. Dress the wounds you know about, then search the whole body, including the back, armpits, groin, and scalp, for wounds you missed. Cover burns with dry, clean dressings (medical-017). Splint fractures and recheck the pulse below the splint (medical-018). Talk to the casualty and explain what you are doing - it calms them and helps you track their alertness.

steps.title: Medications are for trained medics
steps.body: TCCC includes prescription drugs such as tranexamic acid (TXA), antibiotics, ketamine, and blood products. The guidelines say TXA should be given as soon as possible and no later than 3 hours after injury, and that cold-stored whole blood is now the preferred fluid for shock. These are given only by trained, authorized medical personnel under protocols. This app does not give doses. Your job as a first-aider is to stop bleeding, protect the airway, keep the casualty warm, and get them to someone who can give those treatments.

steps.title: Document and hand off
steps.body: Write down what you did and when. The military uses the DD Form 1380 TCCC Card; any paper or tape works. Record tourniquet times (application, any change), wounds, treatments, and repeated checks of pulse, breathing, and alertness. Mark the time on the tourniquet itself. When you hand off, give a short MIST report: Mechanism (what happened), Injuries found, Signs (pulse, breathing, alertness), and Treatments with times. In a civilian emergency call 911 as early as possible, ideally by sending someone else while you work.

steps.title: Tactical Evacuation Care - keep reassessing
steps.body: Moving a casualty can loosen tourniquets, dislodge packing, and change breathing. Before and during any move, recheck every intervention: Is the bleeding still controlled? Is the airway open? Is the person still warm? Keep them wrapped and insulated from the ground or litter. Re-run MARCH from the top whenever something changes, and at least every few minutes for a seriously hurt person. Tell the evacuation team about tourniquets, packed wounds, and any medicines given.

warnings: Bleeding from arms, legs, and junctional areas is the leading cause of preventable trauma death. Do not let airway or small wounds distract you from heavy bleeding.
Never treat in the open while the threat is still active. Get to cover first.
This guide is an overview, not a course. Take a Stop the Bleed, TECC, or TCCC class and practice with the gear you carry.
Do not give prescription drugs (TXA, antibiotics, strong pain medicine) unless you are trained and authorized.
proTips: Carry at least one commercial tourniquet and one roll of hemostatic or plain gauze where you can reach them with either hand.
Say MARCH out loud as you work. Under stress, saying the steps keeps you from skipping one.
The 2026 guidelines expect trained non-medics to reassess and, under set conditions, convert tourniquets within the first 2 hours. Learn this in a hands-on class before you ever try it.
Civilian equivalents: Stop the Bleed (bleeding control only) and TECC (Tactical Emergency Casualty Care) for police, fire, and EMS.

title: Tourniquet Application
summary: How to place a commercial tourniquet on an arm or leg, on yourself or someone else, to stop life-threatening bleeding - and what to do afterward. Follows current CoTCCC guidelines and Stop the Bleed teaching.

steps.title: Decide if a tourniquet is needed
steps.body: Use a tourniquet for bleeding on an arm or leg that could kill: blood spurting or flowing steadily, blood pooling on the ground, clothing soaked fast, a partly or fully cut-off limb, or bleeding that does not stop with firm direct pressure. Also use one when you cannot hold pressure because you must move, treat other people, or protect yourself. Call 911 or send someone to get help first if you can. Put on gloves if you have them. If you are not sure whether the bleeding is life-threatening and it is on a limb, apply the tourniquet - a tourniquet used for a few hours is far less dangerous than bleeding to death.

steps.title: Pick the spot
steps.body: Place the tourniquet 2 to 3 inches (5 to 8 cm) above the wound - between the wound and the heart - and never directly over a joint such as the knee or elbow. If the wound is just below a joint, go above the joint. When you can see the skin, put the tourniquet on bare skin. If you cannot find the wound quickly, the scene is dangerous, or there are many wounds on the limb, place it high on the upper arm or upper thigh over the clothing, then fix the placement once you are safe. Empty bulky items out of pockets under the strap.

steps.title: Tighten the strap first
steps.body: With a windlass tourniquet (such as a CAT or SOF-T style), slide or wrap the band around the limb, pass the tail through the buckle, and pull it as tight as you possibly can by hand. It should be so tight that you cannot slide the tips of three fingers between the band and the limb. Secure the tail on the hook-and-loop. Most of the squeeze comes from this step - a loose strap means you will run out of windlass turns before the bleeding stops.

steps.title: Twist the windlass until bleeding stops
steps.body: Turn the windlass rod until the bleeding stops completely, not just slows. Usually that takes one to three turns. If you have access, check for a pulse below the tourniquet - there should be none. Warn the person it will hurt a lot; pain is expected and does not mean you did it wrong. Lock the rod in its clip, then cover it with the time strap. A partly tightened tourniquet is dangerous: it can block the veins but not the arteries and make bleeding worse.

steps.title: Mark the time and keep watching
steps.body: Write the time the tourniquet went on (for example 'TQ 14:35') on the tourniquet's label or on the skin with a marker, and on any casualty card. Recheck often, especially after moving the person, for new bleeding or a loosened rod. If bleeding continues after a full tightening, add a second tourniquet right next to the first (just above it) and tighten that one. Leave the tourniquet uncovered by blankets so others can see it.

steps.title: Apply one to yourself
steps.body: Arm: put your hand through the pre-formed loop, slide it 2 to 3 inches above the wound, pull the tail tight with your good hand (pin the tourniquet against your side or a hard surface), then twist and lock the windlass. Leg: wrap the strap around the thigh, pull it tight, brace the leg against the ground or your other knee, twist, and lock. Practice both before you ever need them - one-handed application under stress is hard. Keep your tourniquet in the same, reachable spot every day.

steps.title: Leave it on - and what trained people may do
steps.body: A layperson should leave the tourniquet on and let EMS or a hospital take it off. The 2026 TCCC guidelines allow trained responders to convert a tourniquet to a pressure or hemostatic dressing within about 2 hours, but only if the casualty is not in shock, the wound can be watched closely, and the limb is not amputated. A tourniquet left on for more than 6 hours should not be removed in the field. If evacuation is far off, follow fm-005 and get trained help.

steps.title: Improvised tourniquets - last resort
steps.body: Improvised tourniquets fail often. Use one only if you have no commercial tourniquet and pressure and wound packing (medical-003) are not working. Use a band at least 1.5 to 2 inches wide (a folded triangle bandage, tie, or strip of cloth - never wire, cord, or zip ties). Tie it around the limb above the wound, knot a sturdy stick on top, twist until bleeding stops, then tie the stick down so it cannot unwind. Belts usually cannot be pulled tight enough.

warnings: Do not place a tourniquet over a joint - it will not compress the artery well.
A loose tourniquet is worse than none. Tighten until bleeding stops completely, or add a second tourniquet.
Do not loosen a tourniquet 'to let blood flow' - that is an old idea that causes more blood loss.
Buy tourniquets from trusted sellers; cheap knockoffs often break under load.
proTips: Keep one tourniquet on your body and one in your car or bag. A tourniquet locked in a closet does not help on the street.
Practice with a trainer tourniquet, not your duty one - repeated use wears out the band and windlass.
Stage the tourniquet with the tail partly threaded through the buckle so you can apply it fast with one hand.

title: Wound Packing
summary: Pack a deep, heavily bleeding wound with gauze or clean cloth and hold hard pressure to stop bleeding where a tourniquet will not work. Follows Stop the Bleed and current CoTCCC guidelines.

steps.title: Know when to pack
steps.body: Pack a wound when it is bleeding heavily and is deep enough to put your finger into, and a tourniquet cannot be used or is not available. Common examples are wounds in the groin crease, armpit, side of the neck, buttocks, shoulder, and large wounds high on the thigh. Packing also works on limb wounds when you have no tourniquet. Call 911 or send someone for help first. Put on gloves if you have them; if not, use a plastic bag or several layers of cloth between your hands and the blood.

steps.title: Expose and find the source
steps.body: Cut or pull away clothing so you can see the whole wound. Wipe or scoop out pooled blood and clots quickly so you can see where the blood is coming from. The goal is to put the gauze right on the bleeding vessel, which is usually at the bottom of the wound, not on the skin surface. If something is stuck in the wound, do not pull it out - pack around it (medical-023).

steps.title: Pack to the bottom
steps.body: Push the end of the gauze into the wound with one or two fingers, right onto the bleeding spot, and hold it there. Keep feeding more gauze in, pressing each fold down firmly, until the wound is packed tight and no more will fit. Leave a little gauze sticking out above the skin. Hemostatic gauze (gauze treated with a clotting agent) works best, but plain gauze, a clean T-shirt, or other clean cloth also works - technique matters more than the material. If you run out of gauze, add more cloth on top.

steps.title: Hold hard pressure
steps.body: Put both hands on top of the packed wound, lock your elbows, and lean your body weight onto it. This is hard, painful pressure - warn the person. With hemostatic gauze, hold for at least 3 minutes without lifting to peek. With plain gauze or cloth, hold longer; many courses teach about 10 minutes. If help is coming soon, simply keep holding until they take over. Kneeling on a packed thigh wound can work if you must use your hands elsewhere.

steps.title: Wrap it to keep the pressure on
steps.body: When the bleeding has stopped, wrap a pressure bandage or strips of cloth tightly over the packing to keep it in place. On a limb, check that fingers or toes below stay warm and pink; loosen slightly if they turn blue or cold. Junctional areas (groin, armpit, neck) are hard to wrap - see medical-004 for those. For the neck, never wrap around it.

steps.title: If blood soaks through
steps.body: Do not pull the packing out - that tears away the clot. If blood seeps through, press harder and add more gauze on top. If bleeding keeps going strong, the packing probably missed the source: in that case only, a trained responder may remove the packing and repack directly onto the bleeding point. On a limb, apply a tourniquet above the wound if you have one.

steps.title: Tell the next caregiver
steps.body: Write down which type of gauze is in the wound, how many rolls, and the time. Hemostatic gauze must be removed by medical staff, so they need to know it is there. Keep the person lying down and warm, and watch for shock (medical-006). Do not give food or drink. If help is far away, see medical-024 for cleaning and dressing the wound once the bleeding risk has passed.

warnings: Do not pack wounds that go into the chest or belly cavity - you can push gauze into organs. Cover chest wounds as in medical-005 and belly wounds with a moist, clean dressing.
Do not lift your hands to check the wound during the pressure time - every peek can restart the bleeding.
Wound packing is very painful. Explain what you are doing, and if the person is unconscious, keep checking their breathing as you work.
proTips: Z-folded (accordion) hemostatic gauze is easier to feed into a wound than a tight roll.
Practice on a wound-packing trainer; the hardest part is believing how much gauze a wound will take.
A roll of plain gauze plus a pressure bandage is cheap, lightweight, and works - carry it even if you cannot afford hemostatic gauze.

title: Junctional Hemorrhage Control
summary: Stop heavy bleeding in the groin, armpit, and neck - places where limbs join the body and a limb tourniquet cannot reach. Based on current CoTCCC guidelines and Stop the Bleed.

steps.title: Recognize a junctional wound
steps.body: Junctional areas are the groin crease (where the leg meets the body), the armpit and the top of the shoulder, and the neck. Large arteries and veins run close to the surface there, so bleeding can kill within minutes, and a limb tourniquet cannot be placed above the wound. Signs are steady or spurting blood, a fast-growing pool of blood, or a person who gets pale and confused quickly. Call 911 or send someone for help immediately, and get gloves on if you can do it in seconds.

steps.title: Press first, then pack
steps.body: Clamp a hand straight down on the wound right away to slow the bleeding while you get gauze ready. Then pack the wound tightly as in medical-003: push gauze to the bottom, onto the bleeding spot, and keep filling until no more fits. The current TCCC guidelines call for hemostatic gauze with at least 3 minutes of firm direct pressure. If you have only plain gauze or cloth, use it - packing with any clean material is much better than nothing - and hold pressure longer.

steps.title: Groin wounds
steps.body: Kneel beside the casualty with the person flat on their back. After packing, put the heel of one hand on the packing, the other hand on top, lock your elbows, and lean your full weight straight down. If you must free your hands, you can press a knee onto the packing while watching for renewed bleeding. Bind the packing in place with a pressure bandage wrapped around the thigh and hip in a figure-eight. Trained responders with a junctional tourniquet should apply it as soon as it is ready, following the device instructions.

steps.title: Armpit and shoulder wounds
steps.body: Pack the armpit wound deeply and hold pressure upward and inward against the chest wall. To keep pressure on without your hands, place a firm roll of gauze or cloth on top of the packing, bring the arm down against the side of the chest, and bind the arm to the body with a wrap around the chest. This uses the arm itself as a pressure device. Keep checking that the casualty can still breathe comfortably with the wrap on.

steps.title: Neck wounds
steps.body: Press directly on the wound with your fingers or palm, pack it if it is deep, and keep the pressure on one side only. Never wrap a bandage around the neck - it can choke the person and squeeze off blood to the brain. Keep the airway open: let a conscious person sit up and lean forward so blood drains out of the mouth, or roll an unconscious person onto their side. Neck bleeding needs surgery, so arrange the fastest transport you can.

steps.title: Keep the pressure through evacuation
steps.body: Once bleeding stops, do not remove the packing or lift off to look. Add more gauze on top if blood seeps through, and press harder. Keep the casualty lying flat and warm, watch for shock (medical-006), and write down the time, type of gauze, and amount used. When you move the casualty, someone should keep pressure on the wound the whole way, because moving often restarts junctional bleeding.

warnings: Never put circular pressure around the neck.
Junctional bleeding is a surgical emergency. Field care buys minutes, not a cure - evacuate as fast as possible.
Do not use a limb tourniquet on the groin crease or armpit; it cannot squeeze the artery there.
proTips: XStat-type sponge injectors are listed in TCCC for deep, narrow junctional wounds such as bullet tracks, if you are trained in their use.
Practice packing a groin wound on a trainer - most people stop packing too early.
If you are alone with a groin wound and must call for help, kneel on the packed wound while you use your phone.

title: Chest Wounds and Tension Pneumothorax
summary: Care for open chest wounds and recognize a tension pneumothorax - trapped air that crushes the lung and heart. Covers the 2024 AHA-Red Cross first aid approach and the current CoTCCC guidelines for trained responders.

steps.title: Understand the danger
steps.body: A wound or hard blow to the chest can let air leak into the space around a lung. If the air cannot escape, pressure builds with each breath. This is a tension pneumothorax: the lung collapses, and the pressure pushes on the heart and big veins until blood cannot return to the heart. Without relief the person goes into shock and can die within minutes. It can happen with an open wound, a closed (blunt) injury such as a car crash, or after a wound has been sealed too well.

steps.title: Find all chest wounds
steps.body: Call 911 right away for any chest wound. Expose the chest and back - front, sides, and armpits - and run your gloved hands over areas you cannot see. Any hole between the neck and the belly button can enter the chest. You may hear sucking or bubbling as the person breathes. Keep the person in the position that lets them breathe most easily, usually sitting up or leaning toward the injured side, unless other injuries prevent it.

steps.title: Cover an open chest wound
steps.body: The 2024 AHA-Red Cross first aid guidelines say a layperson may leave an open chest wound uncovered, cover it with a clean, dry dressing that is not airtight, or use a vented chest seal. If you put any dressing on and breathing gets worse, loosen or remove it right away. The TCCC guidelines for trained responders call for a vented chest seal, or a non-vented seal if that is all you have, with close watching afterward. Control bleeding from the wound with direct pressure, but do not pack gauze into a hole in the chest.

steps.title: Watch for tension signs
steps.body: Recheck breathing every few minutes. Warning signs of tension pneumothorax are: breathing that gets harder and faster, rising panic or confusion, a fast weak pulse, pale or bluish skin, and one side of the chest that does not rise. Bulging neck veins and a windpipe pushed to one side are late signs and often hard to see. Any chest-injured person who is getting worse should be treated as a possible tension pneumothorax.

steps.title: Burp or remove the seal
steps.body: If the casualty has a chest seal or dressing and is getting worse, lift one edge of the seal (or remove the dressing) to let trapped air out. You may hear a hiss. Then reapply it, or leave the wound open if breathing improves that way. Repeat whenever symptoms return. This is safe for anyone to do and is often enough until help arrives.

steps.title: Needle decompression - trained personnel only
steps.body: When burping does not help, or there is no open wound, trained medics relieve the pressure with a needle. The current CoTCCC guidelines list two sites: the 5th rib space at the anterior axillary line (side of the chest, roughly level with the nipple), or the 2nd rib space at the midclavicular line, never inside the nipple line. They call for a 14- or 10-gauge needle at least 3.25 inches long, inserted over the top of the lower rib, and repeating at the other site if the first fails. Older guides listed the 2nd rib space first; the current guidelines list the side-of-chest site first. Do not attempt this without hands-on training.

steps.title: Evacuate and keep reassessing
steps.body: Every chest injury needs a hospital. Keep the person sitting up if they breathe better that way, keep them warm, and recheck the seal, breathing, pulse, and alertness at least every 5 minutes. A needle or seal can block with blood, so problems can come back. Tell EMS what you saw, when breathing worsened, and every time you burped the seal.

warnings: Do not use an airtight, fully taped homemade seal and walk away - check it constantly and burp it if breathing worsens.
Needle decompression is an invasive procedure that can injure the heart, lungs, or blood vessels. Only trained, authorized responders should perform it.
A person with a chest wound can look fine at first and crash quickly. Get help early.
proTips: Carry a commercial vented chest seal; they stick far better than tape and plastic on sweaty or bloody skin. Wipe the skin dry first.
Carry two seals - bullet and stab wounds often have an exit wound on the back.
Lying the casualty on the injured side can help the good lung work, if spine injury is not a concern.

title: Shock - Recognition and Management
summary: Spot shock early and give the first aid that helps: stop the bleeding, lay the person flat, keep them warm, and get help. Updated to the 2024 AHA-Red Cross guidance - raising the legs is no longer advised after trauma.

steps.title: Know what shock is
steps.body: Shock means the body's organs are not getting enough blood and oxygen. After an injury the most common cause is blood loss, inside or outside the body. Other causes include severe burns, a tension pneumothorax (medical-005), spinal cord injury, severe infection, severe dehydration, and serious allergic reactions (see medical-042 for epinephrine). After any injury, assume shock is from bleeding until proven otherwise, and look for the bleeding.

steps.title: Spot the early signs
steps.body: Early shock can be easy to miss because the body hides it at first. Look for: anxiety, restlessness, or confusion; a fast pulse (over 100 beats per minute in an adult); fast breathing; pale, cool, sweaty skin; thirst; nausea; and slow color return when you press a fingernail. A person who was talking normally and becomes confused or drowsy is getting worse. Young, fit people can look fairly well until they suddenly crash, so do not be reassured by a calm face after a big injury.

steps.title: Spot the late signs
steps.body: As shock worsens, the pulse at the wrist gets weak or disappears, the skin turns gray or blotchy, breathing becomes shallow, and the person becomes very drowsy or unresponsive. The TCCC guidelines use a returning wrist pulse and improving mental status as signs that treatment is working. A missing wrist pulse in an injured person means life-threatening shock - check again for bleeding and push for the fastest evacuation possible.

steps.title: Stop the bleeding first
steps.body: Nothing treats bleeding shock except stopping the bleeding. Check the whole body, including the back, groin, and armpits. Use a tourniquet for heavy limb bleeding (medical-002), pack deep wounds (medical-003, medical-004), and hold firm pressure on everything else. Bleeding inside the chest, belly, or pelvis cannot be stopped in the field - a swollen, tender, or hard belly, or a painful unstable pelvis after a crash or fall, means the person needs surgery as fast as possible.

steps.title: Lay them flat - do not raise the legs after trauma
steps.body: The 2024 AHA-Red Cross first aid guidelines recommend laying a person in shock flat on their back if they are alert. If they might vomit or you cannot stay with them, use the recovery position (on the side) unless you suspect a spine, hip, or pelvic injury. Raising the feet 6 to 12 inches is now considered only for shock without injury - such as fainting, dehydration, or infection - and only if it does not cause pain. Do not raise the legs of an injured person; it can worsen injuries and has little proven benefit. Let a person with a chest injury sit up if that helps them breathe.

steps.title: Keep them warm
steps.body: Cold blood does not clot well, and injured people lose heat fast, even on a mild day. Get the casualty off the ground with a pad, pack, or blanket under them. Cut away or remove wet clothing, then wrap them in a blanket, sleeping bag, or emergency blanket with a windproof layer on the outside. Cover the head and neck. Keep wrapping even if they say they are fine; the TCCC guidelines treat hypothermia prevention as a core step, not an extra.

steps.title: Watch, record, and evacuate
steps.body: Call 911 or arrange the fastest transport you can. Check pulse, breathing, skin, and alertness every 5 minutes and write them down with the time, so you can tell whether the person is getting better or worse. Talk to them and keep them calm. Do not give food or drink to anyone who is confused, drowsy, badly injured, or likely to need surgery. IV fluids and blood are given only by trained medics; in bleeding shock, they aim for a returning wrist pulse rather than normal blood pressure.

warnings: Raising the legs is no longer recommended for injured people in shock.
Do not give anything by mouth to a confused, drowsy, or seriously injured person - they may choke or vomit.
Shock from internal bleeding cannot be fixed in the field. Evacuate early instead of waiting to see if the person improves.
proTips: Practice finding the wrist (radial) pulse on family members so you can find it quickly under stress.
A cheap emergency blanket plus a trash bag over it blocks wind and wet far better than either alone.
Write vital signs on tape on the casualty's chest or a card - responders can see the trend at a glance.
source: AHA-Red Cross First Aid Guidelines 2024 / CoTCCC TCCC Guidelines (May 2026)

Do not use the recovery position if you suspect a spine, hip, or pelvic injury, unless you must protect the airway.

immediate: Find and stop all bleeding - tourniquet, packing, pressure
Lay them flat on their back; do not raise the legs after an injury
Get them off the ground and wrap them warmly

title: Airway Management Without Equipment
summary: Keep an unconscious or badly hurt person's airway open using your hands and body position. Follows the 2024 AHA-Red Cross first aid guidelines, AHA 2025 CPR guidance, and current CoTCCC airway steps.

steps.title: Check responsiveness and breathing
steps.body: Make sure the scene is safe. Tap the shoulders and shout 'Are you OK?' Look at the chest and face for 5 to 10 seconds. Normal breathing is regular and quiet. Snoring, gurgling, or high-pitched noises mean the airway is partly blocked. Gasping, or no breathing at all, means the person needs CPR now - call 911, put them flat on their back, and start chest compressions (medical-015). Do not waste time on airway positioning when CPR is needed.

steps.title: Open the airway: head-tilt chin-lift
steps.body: In an unconscious person the tongue falls back and blocks the throat. Place one hand on the forehead and tilt the head back gently. Put two fingertips under the bony part of the chin and lift the jaw up. Do not press on the soft tissue under the chin. Breathing often becomes quieter right away. This is the standard method when you do not suspect a neck injury.

steps.title: Open the airway: jaw thrust
steps.body: If a neck injury is possible (fall, crash, diving, blow to the head), kneel above the person's head. Place your fingers behind the angles of the lower jaw on both sides, just below the ears, and push the jaw forward and up while keeping the head still. Your thumbs can rest on the cheekbones. If the jaw thrust does not open the airway, use a gentle head tilt anyway - an open airway matters more than a perfectly still neck.

steps.title: Clear what you can see
steps.body: Look in the mouth. If you see vomit, blood, broken teeth, or food, roll the person onto their side and scoop it out with a gloved finger, or let gravity drain it. Never do blind finger sweeps - you can push an object deeper. If the person is conscious and choking, use back blows and abdominal thrusts instead (medical-016).

steps.title: Use the recovery position
steps.body: If the person is breathing normally but not fully awake, and you do not suspect a spine, hip, or pelvis injury, roll them onto their side. Bend the top knee forward to keep them from rolling, tuck the top hand under the cheek, and tilt the head slightly back so fluids drain out of the mouth. The current TCCC guidelines also place unconscious casualties in the recovery position with the head tilted back. If you suspect a spinal injury, leave the person as found unless they vomit, the airway is blocked, or you must leave them alone; then roll them carefully as a unit (medical-021).

steps.title: Let conscious casualties choose their position
steps.body: A conscious person with face or jaw injuries, or blood in the mouth, will often protect their own airway best by sitting up and leaning forward so blood and saliva drain out. Let them do it - do not force them to lie down. TCCC teaches this for facial trauma. Stay with them and be ready to help if they tire or become drowsy.

steps.title: Keep watching
steps.body: An airway that is open now can block again in seconds, especially when you move the person or they vomit. Recheck breathing at least every few minutes and after every move. If breathing stops or becomes gasping, roll them onto their back and start CPR. Trained responders may use a nasopharyngeal airway (a soft tube in the nose) or suction, but these are not a substitute for positioning and should not be used by untrained people, or by anyone when a skull or face fracture is suspected.

warnings: If the person is not breathing or only gasping, start CPR - do not keep repositioning the airway.
Control life-threatening bleeding at the same time as, or before, airway care in trauma (MARCH).
Never put anything in the mouth of a person having a seizure.
proTips: Practice the recovery position with a family member until you can roll an adult alone in under 30 seconds.
Snoring sounds in an unconscious person are an airway problem, not sleep. Reposition right away.
Carry nitrile gloves in every kit - they make clearing a mouth much easier and safer.

title: Oral Rehydration Therapy
summary: Use oral rehydration salts (ORS) to replace the water and salt lost to diarrhea and vomiting. Commercial packets are best; a carefully measured home mix can buy time until you reach care.

steps.title: Spot dehydration early
steps.body: Watch anyone with diarrhea or vomiting for thirst, dark or scant urine, dry mouth, tiredness, and dizziness when standing. Severe dehydration looks like sunken eyes, very little or no urine for many hours, fast weak pulse, confusion, extreme sleepiness, or inability to drink. In babies, also look for no tears when crying, a sunken soft spot, and fewer wet diapers. Start rehydration at the first loose stool - do not wait for severe signs. Diarrhea kills mainly through fluid and salt loss, so early drinking is the treatment that matters most.

steps.title: Use packaged ORS if you have it
steps.body: Mix commercial ORS packets with boiled or treated water exactly as the package says. CDC advises starting ORS right away when cholera is suspected, even while traveling to a clinic. Packets are light, cheap, and shelf-stable, so stock several per person. Do not mix ORS into milk, soup, juice, or soda, and do not add extra sugar. Juice, soft drinks, and sports drinks are high in sugar and can make diarrhea worse. If you have no ORS at all, safe water and broth are better than nothing while you make or find ORS.

steps.title: Make a home mix only if no packets exist
steps.body: Measure precisely: 6 level teaspoons of sugar and 1/2 level teaspoon of salt dissolved in 1 liter (about 1 quart or 5 cups) of clean, boiled-and-cooled or treated water. Use flat, level teaspoons - not heaping. Taste it: it should taste no saltier than tears. Too much salt is dangerous and can cause seizures in a child; too much sugar worsens diarrhea. Too much water is safe, so if in doubt, dilute. Do not boil the finished mix. Keep it cool and make a fresh batch every 24 hours. Health agencies treat home mixes as a stopgap, not a replacement for real ORS.

steps.title: Give small sips often
steps.body: Offer sips every few minutes from a cup or spoon rather than big gulps. As a guide, give children under 2 about 1/4 to 1/2 cup (50-125 ml) after each watery stool, children 2 and older 1/2 to 1 cup (125-250 ml) after each stool, and older children and adults as much as they want - at least 3 quarts (3 liters) a day while diarrhea lasts. If the person vomits, wait 10 minutes, then start again with smaller, slower sips. Most vomiting settles once fluids start going down slowly.

steps.title: Keep feeding
steps.body: Do not starve someone with diarrhea. Keep breastfeeding babies and keep giving formula. Once the person can eat, offer normal, easy foods in small amounts - rice, potatoes, bread, bananas, cooked cereals, and soups. Food helps the gut recover and prevents weakness. WHO and UNICEF also recommend zinc for children with diarrhea, which a health worker can provide. Do not give anti-diarrhea medicines to children unless a trained health worker advises it.

steps.title: Check that it is working
steps.body: Signs of improvement are passing light-colored urine again, better alertness, moist mouth, and tears returning. Keep a simple log of stools, vomiting, and drinks taken. If the person is producing urine regularly and staying alert, keep going with ORS until diarrhea stops. Continue ORS for every watery stool even after the person looks better, because losses continue until the illness ends.

steps.title: Know when ORS is not enough
steps.body: Get medical care urgently for bloody diarrhea, high fever, yellow skin or eyes, vomiting that will not stop, a person too sleepy or weak to drink, no urine for 8 hours or more, or no improvement after a day of good ORS use. Diarrhea lasting more than 3-4 days also needs evaluation. Severely dehydrated people may need IV fluids, but should keep sipping ORS on the way and as soon as they can.

warnings: Measure salt exactly - an over-salted home mix can cause dangerous sodium levels and seizures, especially in small children.
A person who is unconscious, seizing, or too drowsy to swallow must not be given fluids by mouth - get emergency help.
Bloody diarrhea, high fever, or nonstop vomiting means ORS alone is not enough - seek care.
Sugary drinks like juice, soda, and sports drinks are not ORS and can worsen diarrhea.
proTips: Store WHO-formula ORS packets in your kit - they weigh almost nothing and remove the guesswork of home mixing.
Mark a 1-liter bottle with a fill line so you always mix home ORS with the right amount of water.
A spoon and patience work better than a bottle for a vomiting child - one spoonful every minute adds up fast.
Treat or boil the water first; ORS made with contaminated water spreads the illness you are trying to treat.

Do not rely on a home mix when commercial ORS is available.
Do not keep treating at home when there is bloody diarrhea, high fever, or no urine for 8+ hours - get care.

immediate: Mix commercial ORS with treated water per the packet
No packets: 6 level tsp sugar + 1/2 level tsp salt in 1 liter clean water
Give small sips every few minutes; after vomiting wait 10 minutes and restart

Get care for blood in stool, high fever, nonstop vomiting, or no urine

title: Field Sanitation and Latrine Construction
summary: Site and build latrines, hand-washing stations, and gray-water pits that keep human waste away from food and water. Poor sanitation spreads diarrheal disease fast in any camp or grid-down household.

steps.title: Understand the threat
steps.body: Diarrhea, dysentery, typhoid, cholera, and hepatitis A all spread when tiny amounts of feces reach mouths through hands, flies, water, soil, or food. In crowded camps these illnesses can disable a whole group within days, and they combine badly with heat and short water supplies. The U.S. Army assigns trained field sanitation teams to every unit because disease, not injury, has historically taken out more people in the field. Your job is to break every path from waste to mouth: contain waste, wash hands, protect water, and control flies.

steps.title: Pick the site first
steps.body: Before anyone digs, choose the latrine spot. Army field sanitation standards place latrines at least 100 feet (30 m) from any water source, at least 100 yards (90 m) downwind of the kitchen or food area, and about 30 yards (27 m) from the edge of the living area. Downhill from wells and springs is critical, because runoff and groundwater carry contamination. Many backcountry programs use 200 feet (60 m) from water as a simple rule for individuals; use the larger distance when you can. Mark a lit or clearly flagged path for night use.

steps.title: Cat holes for short stops
steps.body: For one person or a group on the move, dig a cat hole for each use. Army guidance calls for about 1 foot (30 cm) deep and wide; outdoor-recreation guidance commonly uses 6-8 inches (15-20 cm) in active topsoil. Either works if waste is fully covered. After use, fill the hole completely, pack the soil down, and mark or disguise it. Pack out or bury toilet paper deep; never leave it on the surface where animals and rain expose it.

steps.title: Straddle trench for a few days
steps.body: For a group staying up to about 3 days, dig straddle trenches about 1 foot (30 cm) wide, 2.5 feet (75 cm) deep, and at least 4 feet (1.2 m) long; each 4-foot trench serves about two people at a time. Space trenches 2 feet (60 cm) apart and give men and women separate, screened areas for privacy and safety. Leave the dug soil beside the trench with a shovel so each user covers their waste right away. Close the trench when waste is within 1 foot (30 cm) of the surface.

steps.title: Deep pit for longer stays
steps.body: For stays longer than about 3 days, dig a deep pit about 2 feet (60 cm) wide, planning roughly 1 foot (30 cm) of depth per week of use plus 1 foot for the final cover. Build a box seat with tight-fitting lids so flies cannot get in or out. Keep lids closed. Where the water table is high or soil is rocky, use bucket toilets with bags and a cover material such as sawdust or soil, and bury or haul the waste to a safe site.

steps.title: Put a hand-wash station at every latrine
steps.body: Set a hand-washing device right outside each latrine and keep it stocked with water and soap at all times. A jug with a spigot, a tippy-tap, or a can with a nail hole all work. Wet hands, lather with soap, scrub all surfaces for about 20 seconds, rinse, and air dry or use a personal towel. Make washing mandatory after latrine use and before handling food. A station that is empty even once a day becomes a disease source.

steps.title: Handle gray water and close latrines properly
steps.body: Pour wash and kitchen water into a soakage pit - a hole filled with rocks or rubble - away from water sources, never into streams. Strain food scraps out first to avoid attracting flies and rodents. To close a latrine, fill with soil in layers, tamping as you go, mound it about 1 foot (30 cm) above ground, and post a marker with the date so no one digs there later.

warnings: Never site a latrine uphill of or within 100 feet (30 m) of a well, spring, or stream.
Open defecation around camp spreads disease to everyone - enforce latrine use for all ages.
Do not burn waste in or near shelters; smoke and fumes are toxic.
Anyone with diarrhea or vomiting must not prepare food for others.
proTips: Keep a shovel and a bag of soil, ash, or sawdust at every latrine so covering waste takes no effort.
Fly-tight lids matter as much as depth - flies carry waste straight to food.
Assign a rotating sanitation duty to check soap, water, lids, and trench depth every day.
Kids follow routines - walk them through the latrine-then-wash habit until it sticks.

Do not use cat holes for a group staying in one place for days - concentrated holes contaminate the area; build a trench.

immediate: Site latrines 100+ ft from water, downhill and 100 yards downwind of food areas
Dig a straddle trench (1 ft wide, 2.5 ft deep, 4 ft long) and leave soil and a shovel beside it
Set up a stocked soap-and-water hand-wash station at the latrine exit
then: Cover waste after every use and keep lids fly-tight
Close trenches 1 ft from the top, mound, and mark them

title: Vector Control - Mosquitoes, Ticks, and Rodents
summary: Cut your risk of mosquito-, tick-, and rodent-borne disease with EPA-registered repellents, standing-water control, daily tick checks, and safe rodent cleanup.

steps.title: Remove mosquito breeding water
steps.body: Mosquitoes lay eggs in almost any still water: buckets, tarps, tires, bottle caps, clogged gutters, and rain barrels without screens. Walk the camp or yard every few days and dump, cover, or screen anything holding water. Fit rain barrels with fine mesh lids. Camp on higher, breezy ground away from marshes when you can. Fixing breeding sites protects the whole group, while repellent only protects the person wearing it.

steps.title: Use an EPA-registered repellent correctly
steps.body: CDC recommends EPA-registered repellents containing DEET, picaridin, IR3535, oil of lemon eucalyptus (OLE), para-menthane-diol (PMD), or 2-undecanone. Follow the label for how much and how often. Put sunscreen on first, then repellent. Do not use OLE or PMD products on children under 3. Do not put repellent on a child's hands, eyes, mouth, or on cuts; spray it on your own hands and then apply to the child's face. Cover strollers and cribs with mosquito netting.

steps.title: Add clothing and nets
steps.body: Wear long sleeves and long pants, light colors, and socks, and tuck pants into socks in tick country. Permethrin is registered for treating clothing, boots, tents, and bed nets - follow the product label and never apply it to skin. Sleep under an intact bed net tucked under the mattress or pad, especially where malaria or dengue exist. Repair holes in screens and nets right away; a single gap lets mosquitoes in all night.

steps.title: Check for ticks every day
steps.body: After time in grass, brush, or woods, check your whole body and your children: scalp, behind ears, neck, armpits, belly button, waist, groin, and behind knees. Check pets and gear too. If you find an attached tick, remove it right away with fine-tipped tweezers, grasping close to the skin and pulling upward with steady, even pressure. Do not use heat, petroleum jelly, or nail polish. See guide medical-051 for full removal and illness signs.

steps.title: Keep rodents out
steps.body: Rodents carry hantavirus, leptospirosis, and other diseases, and they contaminate food. Store food, seed, and pet food in hard, sealed containers off the floor. Remove trash and food scraps daily. Clear brush, woodpiles, and junk away from shelters, and seal gaps in walls with steel wool or metal flashing. Trap rodents with snap traps placed along walls rather than leaving poison where children or pets can reach it.

steps.title: Clean rodent droppings the safe way
steps.body: Never sweep or vacuum droppings or nests - that throws virus particles into the air. Open doors and windows for 30 minutes and leave the area first. Wear rubber or plastic gloves. Soak droppings, urine, and nests with a bleach solution of 1 part bleach to 9 parts water (about 1.5 cups bleach per gallon), mixed fresh, and let it sit 5 minutes or as long as the disinfectant label says. Wipe up with paper towels, double-bag dead rodents and nests, then disinfect surfaces, wash gloved hands, remove gloves, and wash bare hands.

steps.title: Watch for illness afterward
steps.body: Fever, headache, body aches, rash, or trouble breathing in the days to weeks after bites or rodent exposure needs medical care. Tell the clinician about mosquito, tick, or rodent contact and where it happened. Hantavirus can start like flu and then cause severe breathing problems, so shortness of breath after cleaning a rodent-infested space is an emergency.

warnings: Never sweep or vacuum rodent droppings or nests dry - wet them with disinfectant first.
Do not use OLE or PMD repellents on children under 3; follow every product label.
Permethrin is for clothing and gear only - do not apply it to skin.
Shortness of breath after rodent exposure can be hantavirus - get emergency care.
proTips: Use EPA's repellent search tool to compare products by active ingredient and protection time.
Treat clothing and nets before you need them; it is hard to do in the field.
Make tick checks part of the evening routine, like brushing teeth.
Keep a labeled spray bottle and gloves in your kit just for rodent cleanup.
source: CDC / EPA / AHA-Red Cross First Aid 2024

immediate: Dump or cover all standing water around camp

title: Food Safety and Spoilage Identification
summary: Keep food safe when the power goes out: know how long the fridge and freezer hold, when to throw food away, and why smell and looks cannot prove food is safe.

steps.title: Prepare before the outage
steps.body: Keep an appliance thermometer in both the refrigerator and freezer. The fridge should be at 40°F (4°C) or below and the freezer at 0°F (-18°C) or below. Freeze containers of water or gel packs to fill empty freezer space and to use in coolers. Know where to get ice or dry ice. Keep a supply of shelf-stable food that needs no refrigeration so you are not tempted to eat questionable leftovers.

steps.title: Keep the doors shut
steps.body: When power fails, open the fridge and freezer only when you must. A closed refrigerator keeps food safe for about 4 hours. A full closed freezer holds about 48 hours; a half-full one about 24 hours. About 50 pounds (23 kg) of dry ice can keep an 18-cubic-foot freezer cold for roughly 2 days. Handle dry ice with gloves, never bare hands, and do not let it touch food directly or use it in a closed room.

steps.title: Move food to coolers if the outage drags on
steps.body: If power will be out longer than 4 hours, move milk, meat, poultry, fish, eggs, and leftovers into coolers packed with ice or frozen gel packs. Keep the cooler at 40°F (4°C) or below, check with a thermometer, and add ice as it melts. Keep coolers in shade and closed. Group foods so you open the lid briefly and only once.

steps.title: Decide what to keep and what to toss
steps.body: After 4 hours without power, throw out refrigerated perishables - meat, poultry, fish, eggs, soft cheese, cooked leftovers, cut fruit, and dairy - unless a thermometer shows they stayed at 40°F (4°C) or below. Frozen food that still has ice crystals or reads 40°F or below can be refrozen or cooked. Bacteria grow fastest between 40°F and 140°F (4-60°C); food left in that range more than 2 hours (1 hour above 90°F/32°C) is unsafe. When in doubt, throw it out.

steps.title: Do not trust smell, looks, or taste
steps.body: Slime, mold, sour smells, and color changes mean spoilage, so discard food that shows them. But the germs that make people sick - such as Salmonella, E. coli, and Listeria - often cause no change you can see or smell. Never taste food to test it. A bad smell proves a problem; a good smell proves nothing. Mold on soft foods spreads below the surface, so throw out soft moldy foods entirely.

steps.title: Handle cans and floodwater with care
steps.body: Throw away cans that are bulging, leaking, deeply dented along a seam, or that spurt liquid when opened - these can signal botulism, a rare but deadly toxin. Do not taste the contents. Discard any food, including sealed packages and home-canned jars, that touched floodwater. Undamaged commercial metal cans exposed to floodwater can be saved only if labels are removed and cans are washed and sanitized.

steps.title: Cook and serve safely without power
steps.body: Wash hands before handling food. Cook meat and leftovers thoroughly on a stove or grill outdoors - never run grills or camp stoves indoors because of carbon monoxide. Cook only what you will eat right away and do not save leftovers without cold storage. Keep raw meat away from ready-to-eat food. Anyone with diarrhea or vomiting should not cook for others. Watch for signs of botulism - blurred or double vision, drooping eyelids, trouble swallowing or speaking, and weakness spreading downward - and get emergency care at once if they appear.

warnings: Never taste food to see if it is safe.
Bulging or leaking cans may contain botulism toxin - do not open or taste; bag and discard.
Food that touched floodwater must be thrown away unless it is in an undamaged commercial metal can that you wash and sanitize.
Never cook indoors with grills, camp stoves, or generators - carbon monoxide kills.
proTips: A $5 appliance thermometer turns guesswork into a clear keep-or-toss decision.
Tape a note with the time the power went out to the fridge door.
Eat refrigerated perishables first, then freezer food, then shelf-stable supplies.
Frozen water jugs double as drinking water once they thaw.
source: USDA FSIS / FoodSafety.gov

sources.title: Avoid Foodborne Illness During Temporary Power Outages

whenNotTo: Do not refreeze food that has warmed above 40°F (4°C) for more than 2 hours.
Do not use the 'smell test' as proof that meat, dairy, or leftovers are safe.

quickGlance.situation: The power is out and you need to decide what food is still safe to eat.
immediate: Keep fridge and freezer doors closed
Fridge holds about 4 hours; full freezer about 48, half-full about 24
Move perishables to iced coolers at 40°F or below if the outage runs long
then: Toss perishables above 40°F for over 2 hours - when in doubt, throw it out
Discard bulging cans and anything touched by floodwater

title: Combat Stress Reaction - Recognition and Management
summary: Recognize acute stress reactions in yourself and others after a disaster, attack, or loss, and use psychological first aid and the military BICEPS principles to help people recover and function.

steps.title: Know what you are seeing
steps.body: A combat or acute stress reaction is a common response to overwhelming danger, loss, or exhaustion. It is not weakness or a sign of mental illness, and most people recover with support. Military medicine reports that most service members with stress reactions return to duty when handled well. Reactions are different from PTSD, which is a longer-lasting condition diagnosed weeks or more after trauma. Lack of sleep, hunger, dehydration, and cold make stress reactions far more likely.

steps.title: Recognize the signs
steps.body: Physical signs include shaking, jumpiness, a dazed or distant stare, fatigue, stomach upset, headache, and trouble eating or sleeping. Thinking signs include confusion, poor concentration, trouble making decisions, memory gaps, intrusive memories, and nightmares. Emotional signs include irritability, fear, guilt, numbness, withdrawal, crying, and panic. Some people freeze; others become reckless. Any talk of harming self or others is a red flag that needs immediate attention.

steps.title: Make contact and make it safe
steps.body: Psychological first aid, developed by the National Center for PTSD and partners, starts with contact and engagement. Approach calmly, introduce yourself, and ask how you can help. Move the person away from the immediate danger or chaos if you can. Get them physically safe, warm or cool as needed, fed, and hydrated. Speak simply and slowly. Do not force them to describe what happened - let them talk if they want to.

steps.title: Stabilize and calm
steps.body: If someone is panicking or frozen, help them ground: have them notice their feet on the floor, name things they can see, and take slow breaths with you - in through the nose, out longer through the mouth. Give short, clear information about what is happening and what comes next. Uncertainty feeds fear. Keep them near people they trust rather than alone.

steps.title: Apply the BICEPS principles
steps.body: Military combat stress control uses BICEPS: Brevity - keep the intervention short, hours to a few days. Immediacy - help right away. Centrality - support happens close to the group, not far away. Expectancy - tell the person clearly that this reaction is normal and they will recover and rejoin the group. Proximity - keep them near their team or family. Simplicity - focus on sleep, food, water, hygiene, and a chance to talk. These ideas work for civilian groups too.

steps.title: Give practical help and a role
steps.body: Ask what they need most right now and help solve one concrete problem - finding family, water, a dry place to sleep. Once rested, give a simple, useful task such as filling water containers or keeping watch with a partner. Having a job rebuilds a sense of control and competence. Protect sleep with rotation schedules so everyone gets a real rest block.

steps.title: Connect and follow up
steps.body: Help people reconnect with family, friends, faith community, or teammates. Check in again over the next days. Most reactions fade within days to a few weeks. Seek professional help if symptoms last more than a month, get worse, or interfere with daily life, or if there is heavy drinking or drug use. For any thoughts of suicide, call or text 988 (the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline; veterans press 1) or 911.

warnings: Never shame or mock a stress reaction - it deepens the injury and destroys trust.
Talk of suicide or harming others is an emergency - do not leave the person alone; call 988 or 911.
Do not force anyone to retell the event in detail right away; it can make some people worse.
Confusion after a blast, fall, or blow to the head may be a brain injury, not just stress - get medical evaluation.
proTips: Sleep is the strongest treatment - even a few hours of protected sleep can transform someone.
Say the expectancy message out loud: 'This is a normal reaction. You will get through this. We need you back.'
Leaders model calm - your tone of voice spreads through the group.
Pair people up so no one carries the night watch or bad news alone.
source: VA National Center for PTSD (Psychological First Aid) / U.S. military combat stress control

whenNotTo: Do not treat a person with possible head injury, low blood sugar, or poisoning as 'just stressed' - rule out medical causes first.
Do not keep someone in the group role if they are a danger to themselves or others - get professional help.

quickGlance.situation: Someone is shaking, frozen, confused, or emotionally overwhelmed after a traumatic event.
immediate: Move them away from the chaos and make them physically safe
Give water, food, warmth, and a calm voice
Tell them this is a normal reaction and they will recover
then: Protect their sleep and give a simple task when ready
Get help if symptoms last over a month or there is any talk of suicide (988)

title: Long-Term Patient Care Without Resupply
summary: Care for a sick or bedridden person for days or weeks when help is delayed: a clean sick bay, written vital-sign checks, fluids and food, pressure-sore prevention, hygiene, and knowing when to evacuate.

steps.title: Set up a sick bay
steps.body: Pick a dry, sheltered, well-ventilated spot away from the kitchen and food storage. Raise the patient off the ground on a cot or thick padding and keep bedding clean and dry. Put a hand-wash station, a waste bucket with a lid, and a light source within reach. Limit visitors if the illness may be contagious, and have caregivers wash hands before and after every contact. A warm, dry patient recovers far better than a cold, damp one.

steps.title: Check and write down vital signs
steps.body: At least every 4 hours, record the time, pulse, breathing rate, temperature if you have a thermometer, alertness (alert, confused, only responds to voice or pain, or unresponsive), pain level 0-10, fluids in, and urine out. Normal adult resting pulse is about 60-100 per minute and breathing about 12-20. Writing it down lets anyone on the next shift see trends. A rising pulse and breathing rate, new confusion, or falling urine output warns of worsening illness before it is obvious.

steps.title: Keep fluids and food going
steps.body: Dehydration kills faster than hunger. Offer fluids every 30-60 minutes while awake - water, broth, or oral rehydration solution (see medical-008). Fever, diarrhea, and heat increase needs. Aim for light-yellow urine. As appetite returns, give small, frequent meals with protein and calories. Never give food or drink to someone who cannot stay awake or swallow safely; prop alert patients upright to eat.

steps.title: Prevent pressure sores
steps.body: Bedridden people get pressure injuries quickly over bony areas: tailbone, hips, heels, elbows, shoulder blades, spine, and the back of the head. Change their position about every 1-2 hours in bed. If they sit in a chair, have them shift weight every 15-20 minutes. Pad between knees and ankles, float heels on a pillow under the calves, and keep the head of the bed no higher than about 30 degrees when possible. Use a draw sheet to move them instead of dragging. Check the skin daily for redness, warmth, firm or spongy spots, or breaks.

steps.title: Keep the patient clean and dry
steps.body: Wash skin gently each day, especially skin folds and the groin, and clean promptly after urine or stool. Pat dry; moisture breaks skin down fast. Change wet bedding at once. Brush teeth or swab the mouth to prevent mouth infections and pneumonia. Help with deep breaths and coughing several times a day, and get the patient sitting up or walking as soon as it is safe to reduce clots and lung infections.

steps.title: Manage pain and wounds sensibly
steps.body: Use over-the-counter pain relievers only as the label directs, and record every dose and time so doses are not doubled across shifts. Clean wounds with safe water, cover them, and change dressings when wet or dirty. Watch for spreading redness, swelling, pus, red streaks, fever, or chills. Antibiotics require a clinician's direction; misuse can cause harm. See medical-058 for infection and sepsis warning signs.

steps.title: Protect the caregivers and plan evacuation
steps.body: Rotate caregivers so no one goes without sleep, and do a clear handoff each shift: what was given, when, and what changed. Exhausted caregivers make dosing errors and miss danger signs. Decide ahead of time what will trigger evacuation or a call for help - for example, new confusion, trouble breathing, no urine for 8 hours, signs of sepsis, or uncontrolled pain - and keep transport options and contacts ready.

warnings: New confusion, fast breathing, clammy skin, or very low urine output can mean sepsis or shock - seek emergency care.
Do not give oral food or fluids to someone who cannot stay awake or swallow.
Do not give prescription antibiotics or other prescription drugs without a clinician's direction.
Keep a written medication log - double dosing is a common caregiver error.
proTips: Use a whiteboard or notebook taped near the bed as the single source of truth.
Set a turning schedule with a clock face drawn on paper: back, left, right.
A plastic sheet under a cotton sheet protects the bedding without trapping moisture against the skin.
Bring the patient into daily routines - talking, light tasks, daylight - to help mood and recovery.

whenNotTo: Do not keep a patient at home when evacuation or EMS is available and danger signs appear.
Do not move a person with a suspected spine injury for turning without a trained log-roll team.

quickGlance.situation: You are caring for a sick or bedridden person for days without professional help.
immediate: Set up a warm, dry, clean sick bay with a hand-wash station
Record pulse, breathing, temperature, alertness, fluids, and urine every 4 hours
Offer fluids every 30-60 minutes while awake
then: Turn bedridden patients every 1-2 hours and check skin daily
Evacuate or call for help at new confusion, breathing trouble, or no urine

title: Mass Casualty Triage - START Protocol
summary: Sort many injured people fast with START (Simple Triage and Rapid Treatment) so the few rescuers you have reach the people who can be saved first.

steps.title: Make the scene safe and call for help
steps.body: Do not become a casualty. Check for fire, traffic, collapse, downed power lines, or ongoing violence before you go in. Call 911 or your local emergency number, and report the location, type of incident, and rough number of injured. Wear gloves if you have them. Triage means accepting that you cannot treat everyone at once; START lets you spend under a minute per person and find the most urgent cases quickly. START was created in 1983 by Newport Beach, California fire and hospital staff and is still the most widely used mass casualty triage system in the U.S.

steps.title: Sort the walking wounded
steps.body: Shout clearly: 'If you can walk, come to me' or point to a safe, marked area. Everyone who can walk there is GREEN (Minor). Their injuries are unlikely to get worse quickly. Ask a capable green person to help watch the others and report anyone who gets worse. Walking people still need a recheck later; some hide serious injuries.

steps.title: Check breathing
steps.body: Go to each person who did not walk, one at a time, nearest first. Look for breathing. If they are not breathing, open the airway once with a head tilt and chin lift (or jaw thrust if spine injury is likely). If they start breathing, tag them RED (Immediate). If they still do not breathe after one airway reposition, tag them BLACK (Expectant/Deceased) and move on. If they are breathing, estimate the rate: more than 30 breaths per minute is RED.

steps.title: Check circulation
steps.body: If breathing is under 30 per minute, check perfusion. Feel for a pulse at the wrist (radial pulse) or press a fingernail and see if color returns within 2 seconds. No radial pulse, or capillary refill longer than 2 seconds, is RED. The 1996 revision of START favored the radial pulse because capillary refill is unreliable in cold or dark conditions. If you see major bleeding, control it now with direct pressure or a tourniquet, then keep going.

steps.title: Check mental status
steps.body: If breathing and circulation pass, give a simple command: 'Squeeze my hand' or 'Open your eyes.' If the person cannot follow simple commands, tag them RED. If they can follow commands, tag them YELLOW (Delayed). Yellow patients may have serious injuries but are not expected to worsen significantly over the next hour or more.

steps.title: Tag and keep moving
steps.body: Mark each person clearly with colored tape, a tag, or marker on the forehead or arm: R, Y, G, or B (or DEAD/EXP). The only treatments during triage are opening an airway and stopping major bleeding - do not stop to do full care, splint, or bandage minor wounds. Keep a quick tally of how many in each color for arriving responders. Aim for 30-60 seconds per person.

steps.title: Treat, reassess, and hand off
steps.body: Once everyone is tagged, send helpers to RED patients first, then YELLOW, then GREEN. Patients change - recheck everyone every 15-30 minutes and re-tag as needed. Expectant patients deserve comfort and pain relief when resources allow; this is not abandonment but the hard reality of too many patients for too few rescuers. When EMS arrives, report your counts and the location of each RED patient.

warnings: Do not tag a non-breathing person BLACK until you have repositioned the airway once.
Do not stop to give full treatment during the triage sweep - only airway and major bleeding control.
Adult START criteria do not fit small children well; pediatric versions such as JumpSTART exist.
Re-triage often - a YELLOW can become RED in minutes.
proTips: Carry a roll each of red, yellow, and green tape plus a marker in your vehicle kit.
Count breaths for 15 seconds and multiply by 4 - fast enough for triage.
Use a green helper as a runner to bring supplies and report changes.
Practice the sequence out loud: Walk - Breathe - 30 - Pulse - Command.

immediate: Call 911; tell everyone who can walk to move to a safe spot - they are GREEN

No radial pulse or refill over 2 sec: RED; cannot follow commands: RED; otherwise YELLOW
then: Treat RED first, then YELLOW, then GREEN
Recheck and re-tag everyone every 15-30 minutes

title: CPR and AED - Adult, Child, and Infant
summary: How to give high-quality CPR and use an AED for adults, children, and infants, following the 2025 American Heart Association guidelines - including the end of two-finger infant compressions.

steps.title: Check the scene and the person
steps.body: Make sure the scene is safe for you - traffic, fire, electricity, water. Tap the person's shoulders (for an infant, tap the foot) and shout 'Are you OK?' Look at the chest and face for 5 to 10 seconds. If they are not breathing, or only gasping, they are in cardiac arrest. Gasping is not normal breathing - it is a sign to start CPR, not to wait.

steps.title: Call for help and get an AED
steps.body: Shout for help. If you have a phone, call 911 and put it on speaker so the dispatcher can coach you while you work. Send anyone nearby to bring an AED. If you are alone with no phone and the person is an adult, leave them to call 911 and get an AED first, then start CPR (2025 AHA guidance). For a child or infant, or anyone who was drowning, give about 2 minutes of CPR first (5 rounds of 30 compressions and 2 breaths), then go call - their arrest usually starts with a breathing problem, so early breaths matter most.

steps.title: Give chest compressions
steps.body: Lay the person on their back on a firm surface; if they are on a bed or couch, start right away and push harder rather than wasting time moving them. Adult: put the heel of one hand on the center of the chest (lower half of the breastbone), other hand on top, arms straight, shoulders over your hands. Push at least 2 inches (5 cm) deep, but not more than about 2.4 inches (6 cm). Child (1 year to puberty): one or two hands, about 2 inches (5 cm), at least one-third the depth of the chest. For all ages, push at 100 to 120 per minute, let the chest come all the way back up, and do not stop for more than 10 seconds.

steps.title: Infants: heel of one hand or two thumbs
steps.body: The 2025 guidelines dropped the old two-finger method because rescuers rarely pushed deep enough with it. For an infant (under 1 year), place the heel of one hand on the center of the chest just below the nipple line, or wrap both hands around the chest and press with both thumbs side by side. Push about 1.5 inches (4 cm) - one-third of the chest depth - at 100 to 120 per minute. Keep the head in a neutral 'sniffing' position, not tilted far back.

steps.title: Give rescue breaths
steps.body: After 30 compressions, give 2 breaths. Tilt the head back and lift the chin, pinch the nose, seal your mouth over theirs, and blow for about 1 second each, just enough to see the chest rise. For an infant, cover both the mouth and nose with your mouth. Use a pocket mask or face shield if you have one. Breaths matter most for children, infants, drowning victims, and suspected opioid overdoses. If you are untrained or unwilling to give breaths to an adult, give continuous compressions - that is far better than doing nothing.

steps.title: Use the AED as soon as it arrives
steps.body: Turn it on and follow the voice prompts. Bare the chest; wipe it dry if wet. Place one pad on the upper right chest below the collarbone and the other on the lower left side below the armpit, or as pictured on the pads. Pads may go under a bra as long as they touch bare skin. For children under 8, use child pads or a pediatric setting if available; if not, adult pads are acceptable - place them so they do not touch, front and back if needed. Make sure nobody touches the person during analysis or shock, then restart compressions immediately after a shock.

steps.title: Keep going and swap rescuers
steps.body: Continue cycles of 30 compressions and 2 breaths until the person starts breathing normally or moving, EMS takes over, an AED tells you to stop, or you are too exhausted to continue. Compressions get shallow after about 2 minutes, so if there are two rescuers, switch every 2 minutes, ideally when the AED analyzes. If the person starts breathing normally, roll them into the recovery position and watch them closely.

steps.title: Special situations
steps.body: Suspected opioid overdose: give CPR with breaths and give naloxone following the package instructions - call 911. Drowning: start with breaths and CPR as soon as the person is out of the water (medical-028). Lightning: start CPR immediately; victims are safe to touch (medical-029). Severe hypothermia: check for a pulse for up to a minute before starting compressions (medical-025). Women in late pregnancy: give normal CPR and have someone push the belly gently to the person's left.

warnings: Do not wait to 'make sure' - if a person is unresponsive and not breathing normally, start compressions.
Shallow compressions do little. Push hard and fast; broken ribs can heal, but no blood flow is fatal.
Never touch the person while an AED is analyzing or shocking.
proTips: Push to the beat of a song around 100-120 beats per minute, such as 'Stayin' Alive.'
Take an AHA or Red Cross class with manikin feedback - most people push too shallow until they feel the correct depth.
Learn where AEDs are mounted at your work, school, gym, and church before you need one.
source: American Heart Association 2025 CPR and ECC Guidelines

whenNotTo: Do not start CPR on someone who is breathing normally or moving - use the recovery position and monitor.
Do not start CPR if the scene is unsafe for you; make it safe or wait for responders.
Do not start CPR when there are obvious signs of death that cannot be reversed, such as decapitation or rigor mortis.

quickGlance.situation: Someone is unresponsive and not breathing, or only gasping.
immediate: Call 911 on speaker and send someone for an AED
Push hard and fast in the center of the chest - 100-120 per minute, 2 inches deep for adults
Give 30 compressions and 2 breaths, or nonstop compressions if you cannot give breaths
then: Turn on the AED as soon as it arrives and follow its prompts
Keep going until the person breathes normally or EMS takes over

title: Choking - Adult, Child, and Infant
summary: Clear a blocked airway using the 2025 American Heart Association sequence: alternate 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts for adults and children, and 5 back blows and 5 chest thrusts for infants.

steps.title: Recognize severe choking
steps.body: A person with a severe blockage cannot speak, cough forcefully, or breathe, and may clutch their throat. They may make a high-pitched noise or no sound at all, and their lips can turn blue. Ask 'Are you choking?' If they nod and cannot talk, act now. If they can cough hard or speak, the blockage is partial: encourage them to keep coughing, stay with them, and be ready to act if the cough becomes weak or silent. Have someone call 911.

steps.title: Adult or child: give 5 back blows
steps.body: The 2025 AHA guidelines added back blows to the adult and child sequence. Stand slightly behind and to the side of the person. Support their chest with one hand and lean them forward so the object comes out of the mouth rather than going deeper. With the heel of your other hand, give up to 5 sharp blows between the shoulder blades. Check after each blow whether the object has come out. For a small child, kneel down to their height.

steps.title: Adult or child: give 5 abdominal thrusts
steps.body: If back blows do not work, stand behind the person and wrap your arms around their waist. Make a fist and place the thumb side just above the belly button, well below the breastbone. Grab the fist with your other hand and give up to 5 quick, hard thrusts inward and upward. Keep alternating 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts until the object comes out or the person becomes unresponsive.

steps.title: Pregnant or large person: chest thrusts
steps.body: If you cannot reach around the person's belly, or they are visibly pregnant, use chest thrusts instead of abdominal thrusts. Stand behind them, put your arms under their armpits, place your fist on the center of the breastbone, and pull straight back sharply. Alternate 5 back blows with 5 chest thrusts. If you are alone and choking, call 911 and give yourself abdominal thrusts with your fist, or thrust your upper belly hard against the back of a chair or a counter edge.

steps.title: Infant: 5 back blows, then 5 chest thrusts
steps.body: For a baby under 1 year, sit or kneel and lay the infant face-down along your forearm, head lower than the chest, supporting the jaw with your hand (do not cover the mouth or throat). Rest your arm on your thigh. Give up to 5 firm back blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand. Then sandwich the baby between your arms, turn them face-up with the head still lower, and give up to 5 chest thrusts on the center of the chest just below the nipple line. The 2025 guidance uses the heel of one hand for these thrusts. Repeat until the object comes out or the baby becomes unresponsive. Never give abdominal thrusts to an infant.

steps.title: If they become unresponsive
steps.body: Lower the person carefully to the ground, call 911 if not done, and start CPR, beginning with chest compressions (medical-015). Each time you open the airway to give breaths, look in the mouth. If you can see the object, remove it with your fingers. Never do blind finger sweeps - you can push it deeper. Continue CPR until the person breathes, EMS arrives, or an AED is available.

steps.title: After the object comes out
steps.body: Anyone who received abdominal or chest thrusts, or who became unresponsive, should be checked by a medical professional - thrusts can injure organs, and pieces of the object can stay in the airway. Watch for ongoing cough, wheezing, trouble swallowing, chest or belly pain, or fever in the following days. In a grid-down setting, keep them resting and observed, and seek care as soon as possible.

warnings: Do not slap the back of someone who can still cough forcefully - let them cough.
Never give abdominal thrusts to an infant under 1 year.
Never do blind finger sweeps in the mouth of an adult, child, or infant.
proTips: Cut grapes, hot dogs, and round candies lengthwise for small children - these are common choking hazards.
Practice finding the hand position on a family member without thrusting.
If you are eating alone, sit where others can see you or near a sturdy chair you could use for self-thrusts.
source: American Heart Association 2025 CPR and ECC Guidelines
