whenNotTo: Do not intervene with blows or thrusts while the person can still cough forcefully or speak.
Do not use abdominal thrusts on infants, or on visibly pregnant or very large people (use chest thrusts).

quickGlance.situation: Someone cannot speak, cough, or breathe after something got stuck in the throat.
immediate: Adult or child: alternate 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts
Infant: alternate 5 back blows and 5 chest thrusts - no abdominal thrusts
Pregnant or large person: alternate back blows with chest thrusts
then: If they go unresponsive, call 911 and start CPR; look in the mouth before breaths
Get a medical check after any thrusts

title: Burns - Thermal, Chemical, and Electrical
summary: Stop the burning, cool the burn with running water for 20 minutes, cover it loosely, and know which burns need emergency care or evacuation. Covers heat, chemical, and electrical burns.

steps.title: Stop the burning safely
steps.body: Protect yourself first. For clothing on fire: stop, drop, and roll, or smother the flames with a heavy blanket. For electrical injuries, turn off the power at the breaker or unplug the device before touching the person; stay far away from downed power lines and call the utility and 911. For chemicals, put on gloves, brush off any dry powder, and then remove contaminated clothing and jewelry. Get the person away from smoke. Call 911 for any large, deep, electrical, chemical, or inhalation burn.

steps.title: Cool heat burns with running water
steps.body: Run cool tap water (not ice-cold) over the burn for 20 minutes, or put the person under a cool shower if the burn is large. Cooling still helps if you start up to 3 hours after the burn. Do not use ice, ice water, butter, oil, toothpaste, or other home remedies. If you have little water, use the cleanest cool water you can and cool the most painful area. While cooling a large burn, keep the rest of the person warm - large burns and small children chill fast.

steps.title: Remove tight items and cover loosely
steps.body: Take off rings, watches, belts, and tight clothing near the burn before swelling starts. Leave anything that is stuck to the skin; cut around it. After cooling, cover the burn loosely with clean plastic wrap laid on in strips (not wrapped tight around a limb), a clean nonstick dressing, or a clean, lint-free cloth. The 2024 AHA-Red Cross guidance says a loose, clean, dry dressing is reasonable while waiting for care. Raise burned arms or legs to limit swelling, and keep a person with face or neck burns sitting up.

steps.title: Chemical burns: flush, flush, flush
steps.body: After brushing off any dry chemical, flush the skin with lots of running water for at least 20 minutes - longer if it still hurts or burns. Use a shower or hose for large areas. Let the runoff flow away from unburned skin and from your own hands. A few metals (sodium, potassium, lithium, magnesium) react with water; if you know one of these is involved, brush it off and get expert advice. Bring the container or chemical name to medical care, and call Poison Help at 800-222-1222 for guidance. For chemicals in the eye, see medical-022.

steps.title: Electrical burns: look deeper
steps.body: Once the power is off, check breathing and pulse - electricity can stop the heart. Start CPR if needed (medical-015). Electrical burns often look small on the skin but cause deep damage to muscles, nerves, and the heart along the current's path. Look for both an entry and an exit wound, often on a hand and a foot. Every electrical injury beyond a minor household shock needs a medical exam, even if the person feels fine. Cover burns with a clean, dry cloth; do not apply ointments or ice.

steps.title: Check for smoke inhalation
steps.body: Anyone burned in a closed space, or with burns on the face, singed nose hairs, soot around the nose or mouth, a hoarse voice, coughing, or trouble breathing, may have airway burns. Swelling can close the airway hours later. Keep them sitting upright, get them to fresh air, and call 911 or evacuate urgently even if they look fine now. Carbon monoxide poisoning can also cause headache, confusion, and vomiting.

steps.title: Decide who needs care or evacuation
steps.body: Get prompt medical care for: deep burns (white, leathery, brown, or painless areas); blistering burns larger than the person's palm; burns on the face, hands, feet, genitals, or major joints; burns that wrap all the way around a limb, the chest, or the neck; chemical, electrical, or inhalation burns; and any burn in a young child, an older adult, or someone with serious health problems. Large burns cause shock (medical-006). In a grid-down situation, these are the burns that justify an evacuation.

steps.title: Care for small burns at home
steps.body: For small, shallow burns (red, or small blisters smaller than the palm), after cooling, cover with a nonstick dressing. The 2024 AHA-Red Cross guidance says petroleum jelly, antibiotic ointment, honey, or aloe vera under a nonstick dressing may be reasonable for small burns. Over-the-counter pain medicine can help - follow the label. Do not pop blisters. Change the dressing daily and watch for infection: spreading redness, swelling, pus, or fever.

warnings: Never touch someone still in contact with electricity. Turn off the power first.
Do not use ice or ice water on burns - it deepens tissue damage and can cause hypothermia.
Burns of the face, nose hair, or mouth can swell the airway closed hours later - treat as an emergency.
proTips: Plastic cling wrap is a great burn cover: clean, nonstick, see-through, and cheap. Lay it on, do not wrap tightly.
If water is scarce, cooling with any clean cool liquid is better than nothing; avoid oils.
Remember the person's palm (including fingers) is about 1% of their body surface - use it to estimate burn size.

immediate: Stop the burning - turn off power, brush off dry chemicals, put out flames
Cool with running water for 20 minutes (no ice)
Remove rings and tight items; cover loosely with plastic wrap or a clean dressing

Keep the person warm and watch for breathing trouble and shock

title: Fractures and Improvised Splinting
summary: Recognize a broken bone, care for open fractures, and build a padded splint from whatever you have - sticks, boards, rolled clothing, or the body itself. Based on U.S. Army first aid training and current first aid guidance.

steps.title: Handle life threats first
steps.body: A broken bone is rarely the most dangerous injury. Check for heavy bleeding, breathing problems, and shock first (medical-031). A broken thigh bone or pelvis can bleed enough inside to cause shock. Call for help. Signs of a fracture are pain at one spot, swelling, bruising, deformity or an odd angle, grinding, loss of use, or bone sticking through the skin. If you cannot tell whether it is a fracture, sprain, or dislocation, treat it as a fracture.

steps.title: Check circulation, sensation, and movement
steps.body: Before you splint, check below the injury: Is the hand or foot warm and normal in color? Does the nail bed pink up within about 2 seconds after you press it? Can the person feel your touch and wiggle their fingers or toes? Write down what you find. A cold, pale, or blue limb, or one that has lost feeling, is an emergency - the bone may be pinching an artery or nerve. Get urgent help; trained responders may gently straighten a badly bent limb to restore blood flow.

steps.title: Cover open fractures - do not push bone back
steps.body: If bone or a deep wound is showing, control bleeding with pressure around the wound (not on the bone end). Do not push the bone back in or try to clean deep inside. Cover the wound and bone with a clean, moist or dry dressing, then splint. Open fractures get infected easily and need a hospital, so evacuate these as a priority. If evacuation will take a long time, rinse visible dirt from the wound with drinkable water (medical-024).

steps.title: Gather splint materials
steps.body: A splint must be rigid and long enough to reach past the joint above and the joint below the break. Good improvised materials: straight sticks, boards, trekking poles, tent poles, rolled magazines or newspapers, cardboard, a folded sleeping pad (SAM-type splints work the same way), or a ski. For padding, use clothing, blankets, a jacket, or leaves. For ties, use cloth strips, triangle bandages, belts, or tape - not wire or thin cord, which can cut off blood flow. If you have nothing rigid, tie the injured leg to the good leg or the injured arm to the chest.

steps.title: Splint it in the position found
steps.body: Move the limb as little as possible and splint it in the position you found it. Have someone hold the limb steady above and below the break. Pad the splint well, especially at bony points such as the wrist, elbow, knee, and ankle, and in the armpit or groin. Place rigid pieces on both sides if you can. Tie them on above and below the break - never directly on top of it. Tie knots on the splint, not on the skin. Snug is enough; you should be able to slip a finger under each tie.

steps.title: Use a sling and swathe for arms
steps.body: For a broken collarbone, upper arm, elbow, forearm, or wrist, support the arm in a sling made from a triangle bandage, a shirt, or by pinning up the bottom of a jacket. Keep the hand slightly higher than the elbow. Then wrap a wide strip of cloth (a swathe) around the arm and chest to hold the arm against the body - above or below the break, never on it. For a broken leg, splint the whole leg including the foot and ankle.

steps.title: Recheck and manage pain
steps.body: Check circulation, sensation, and movement again right after splinting and every 15 minutes. If fingers or toes become numb, tingly, cold, pale, or blue, loosen the ties, add padding, and retie. Apply a cold pack wrapped in cloth for 15 to 20 minutes at a time to reduce swelling, and raise the limb if it does not cause pain. Over-the-counter pain medicine can help; follow the label. Get every suspected fracture checked by a medical professional, and evacuate urgently for open fractures, thigh or pelvis fractures, or a limb without a pulse.

warnings: Do not try to straighten or realign a fracture unless you are trained and the limb has no circulation.
Never push protruding bone back under the skin.
Ties that are too tight can cut off blood flow. Recheck often, because swelling increases for hours.
proTips: A foam sleeping pad rolled into a U-shape makes an excellent lower-leg or arm splint.
Splint before moving the casualty - it reduces pain, bleeding, and further damage.
Remove rings and watches on an injured arm right away, before swelling traps them.

title: Sprains, Strains, and Dislocations
summary: Tell a sprain or strain from something more serious, treat it with rest, ice, compression, and elevation, and protect a dislocated joint without forcing it back in place.

steps.title: Know the difference
steps.body: A sprain is a stretched or torn ligament - the tissue that joins bone to bone at a joint - often an ankle, knee, or wrist after a twist. A strain is a stretched or torn muscle or tendon, often the back, hamstring, or calf. A dislocation is when the bones of a joint come out of their normal position; the joint looks deformed and the person usually cannot move it. Fractures can look like any of these. If you are unsure, or the person cannot bear weight or use the limb, treat it as a fracture and splint it (medical-018).

steps.title: Look for warning signs
steps.body: Get medical care, or treat as a fracture, if: the joint or limb looks bent or deformed; there is a bone tender spot when you press directly on it; the person cannot take four steps or use the hand; the area below is numb, tingling, cold, pale, or blue; the swelling is severe; or there was a popping sound with immediate severe pain. Check feeling, color, and movement below the injury and write it down so you can compare later.

steps.title: Rest and protect
steps.body: Stop the activity and avoid anything that causes pain. Protect the joint with a brace, an elastic wrap, or a splint. For an ankle in the field, leaving the boot on and lacing it snugly can support the joint while the person walks out, if walking is needed for safety; check toes for color and feeling. Use a stick or trekking pole as a cane. Do not 'walk it off' through sharp pain.

steps.title: Ice, compression, and elevation
steps.body: Apply ice or a cold pack wrapped in a thin cloth for 15 to 20 minutes at a time, every 2 to 3 hours while awake, for the first few days. Cold stream water in a bag works too. Never put ice directly on bare skin. Wrap the joint with an elastic bandage starting at the end farthest from the heart and moving upward. Loosen it if pain increases, the area goes numb, or swelling builds below the wrap. Raise the limb above heart level when resting, especially at night.

steps.title: Pain relief and gentle movement
steps.body: Over-the-counter pain relievers such as ibuprofen or acetaminophen can help - follow the label. After the first day or two, start gentle movement within the pain-free range; this usually speeds recovery more than total rest. Healing can take days for a mild sprain and weeks to months for a bad one. Rebuild strength and balance slowly before returning to heavy loads or rough ground.

steps.title: Dislocations: support, do not force
steps.body: Do not try to push a dislocated joint back into place. Doing so can damage nerves, arteries, and bone, and there may be a fracture you cannot see. Support the joint in the position of greatest comfort with a sling, padding, or splint. For a shoulder, let the person hold the arm in the position they choose and pad between the arm and chest with a rolled jacket. Apply a wrapped cold pack and check circulation below the joint often.

steps.title: When help is far away
steps.body: A dislocation with no pulse, or with a cold, blue hand or foot, is an emergency - evacuate urgently. Some wilderness medicine courses teach trained responders to reduce certain simple dislocations (such as a kneecap or a shoulder) when help is days away. That is a skill for a hands-on course, not something to learn from a screen. Everyone with a dislocation should be seen by a medical professional, even if the joint goes back in on its own.

warnings: Do not force a dislocated joint back into place.
Ice directly on skin can cause frostbite - always use a cloth barrier and limit to 20 minutes.
An elastic wrap that is too tight can cut off circulation. Check fingers or toes after wrapping.
proTips: A bag of frozen peas molds around a joint better than a block of ice.
Old ankle sprains get re-injured easily - tape or brace the ankle for rough terrain while it heals.
A triangle bandage in your kit can be a sling, a wrap, or splint ties.

title: Head Injury and Concussion - Danger Signs
summary: What to do after a blow to the head, the CDC danger signs that mean emergency care now, and how to watch someone with a concussion over the next 24-48 hours when help is far away.

steps.title: Make it safe and check the basics
steps.body: After a fall, crash, or blow to the head, stop the activity - no returning to play or work that day. Check responsiveness, breathing, and bleeding. A head blow hard enough to knock someone out can also injure the neck, so keep the head and neck still if the person is confused, unconscious, or complains of neck pain (medical-021). Scalp wounds bleed heavily; press firmly with a clean cloth, but do not press hard on an area that feels soft, dented, or crackly, which may be a skull fracture.

steps.title: Know the danger signs
steps.body: Call 911 or get the person to an emergency department right away for any of these CDC danger signs: seizures; not recognizing people or places; repeated vomiting; unusual behavior, increasing confusion, restlessness, or agitation; loss of consciousness, increasing drowsiness, or being unable to wake up; slurred speech, weakness, numbness, or poor coordination; a headache that keeps getting worse; one pupil larger than the other or double vision. In babies and toddlers, also watch for crying that cannot be calmed and refusing to nurse or eat.

steps.title: Look for other serious signs
steps.body: Other signs of a serious brain or skull injury include clear fluid or blood leaking from the nose or ears, bruising behind the ears or around both eyes, a dent in the skull, or a person who 'talks and then dies' - someone who seems fine after the injury and then becomes drowsy hours later because of bleeding inside the skull. Anyone on blood thinners, any older adult, and anyone who was knocked out should be checked by a medical professional even if they seem well.

steps.title: Recognize a concussion
steps.body: A concussion is a brain injury from a bump, blow, or jolt that shakes the brain. Symptoms include headache, dizziness, balance trouble, nausea, sensitivity to light or noise, blurry vision, feeling foggy or slowed down, memory gaps, trouble concentrating, irritability, sadness, anxiety, and sleep changes. Symptoms may not appear for hours or days and are often worst 1 to 2 days after the injury. Most people do not lose consciousness.

steps.title: Position and protect
steps.body: If the person is unconscious but breathing and you do not suspect a neck injury, place them in the recovery position (medical-007). If they are awake, keep them resting with the head and shoulders raised on a pack or pillow - the TCCC guidelines raise the head and torso of casualties with moderate or severe head injury when they are not in shock. Keep them warm and calm. Do not give alcohol, sleeping pills, or recreational drugs. Stop any bleeding and keep the airway clear if they vomit.

steps.title: Watch them closely for 24-48 hours
steps.body: Do not leave a head-injured person alone for the first 24 hours. They can sleep, but check on them every few hours: they should wake up easily, know who they are and where they are, and speak and move normally. Write down the time and what you find. Any danger sign from step 2 means emergency care, or evacuation if you are off-grid. Acetaminophen used by the label is a reasonable choice for headache; ask a clinician before using aspirin or ibuprofen soon after a head injury, since they can increase bleeding.

steps.title: Recovery and return to activity
steps.body: For the first few days, rest the brain: limit screens, reading, loud noise, and heavy work, but light activity such as walking is usually fine. Return to normal tasks gradually as symptoms allow. Never return to sports, fighting, climbing, or other risky activity until symptoms are gone and, ideally, a healthcare provider clears it - a second blow before healing can cause severe brain swelling. Children and teens often need longer to recover.

warnings: A person who seems fine after a head blow can deteriorate hours later. Do not leave them alone for 24 hours.
Any CDC danger sign means emergency care - do not wait to see if it passes.
Assume a neck injury in anyone knocked out or confused after a significant blow.
proTips: Ask simple orientation questions - name, place, day, what happened - and note the answers each time you check.
Write the time of injury and any loss of consciousness; doctors will ask.
Wear a helmet for biking, climbing, and riding - prevention beats any field treatment.

title: Suspected Spinal Injury - When to Move and How
summary: Protect the spinal cord without making other injuries worse. Reflects the shift in AHA-Red Cross 2024 and Wilderness Medical Society guidance away from rigid collars and backboards toward careful handling and padding.

steps.title: Suspect it from what happened
steps.body: Think spine injury after: falls from height, car or motorcycle crashes, diving into shallow water, being hit by a vehicle, heavy objects falling on someone, or any hard blow to the head or neck. Signs include neck or back pain, tenderness right over the spine, numbness, tingling, or weakness in the arms or legs, loss of bladder control, or an unconscious or confused person after one of these events. Penetrating injuries such as stab or gunshot wounds rarely cause unstable spine damage that handling can worsen; treat their bleeding first.

steps.title: Life threats come first
steps.body: Bleeding, airway, and breathing come before the spine. Never let spine worries delay stopping heavy bleeding, opening an airway, or starting CPR. If you need to roll someone to clear vomit or start CPR, do it - move them as carefully as you can, but do it. The Wilderness Medical Society guidance stresses that shock and lack of oxygen do more harm to an injured spinal cord than a careful move.

steps.title: Leave them as found if possible
steps.body: The 2024 AHA-Red Cross first aid guidelines say to leave a person with a suspected neck, back, hip, or pelvic injury in the position you found them, unless the area is unsafe or you must move them to care for the airway. Call 911. Tell the person not to move their head. Kneel at the head and hold it gently in line with the body with your hands over the ears, or pad around the head with rolled clothing, shoes, or packs. Keep them warm.

steps.title: Alert, reliable people can move themselves
steps.body: Current wilderness guidance trusts an alert, sober, cooperative person to protect their own spine - pain will tell them to stop. If the scene is dangerous, or help is many hours away, such a person can carefully move themselves, with your help steadying them, to a safer or warmer spot. A person who is drunk, high, confused, panicking, or distracted by another painful injury cannot be trusted this way; protect their spine for them.

steps.title: Collars and backboards are no longer required
steps.body: Rigid neck collars and hard backboards used to be standard. The Wilderness Medical Society now says there is no required role for either, and first aid guidance no longer recommends that laypeople apply collars - they can be uncomfortable, raise pressure inside the skull, interfere with the airway, and cause pressure sores. A rolled jacket or towel wrapped loosely around the neck as a soft reminder, plus padding around the head, is enough. If a backboard is used to drag someone out, take them off it as soon as possible.

steps.title: Log roll when you must move them
steps.body: To roll a person onto their side (for vomiting, to place insulation underneath, or to check the back), use at least two helpers and ideally four. The person at the head is in charge: they hold the head in line with the body and count 'one, two, three, roll.' Everyone rolls together so the head, shoulders, and hips turn as one unit, like a log. Slide a pad or blanket under them, then roll back on the same count. The recovery position is acceptable if done with care to limit twisting.

steps.title: Carrying and evacuating
steps.body: If the person cannot walk and must be carried, keep the head, neck, and body in line. A vacuum mattress is the best carrying device; otherwise use a well-padded litter, a blanket stretcher, or a door, with rolled clothing along both sides of the head and body. Insulate from the ground and secure the person so they do not slide. Recheck feeling and movement in the hands and feet before and after any move and write down what you find. Any new weakness or numbness means evacuate urgently.

warnings: Do not delay CPR, bleeding control, or airway care because of a possible spine injury.
Do not pull on the head or force it into line if moving it causes pain, spasm, or new numbness - support it where it is.
Do not remove a motorcycle or football helmet unless you must reach the airway and have training.
proTips: Practice a 4-person log roll with friends before you need it; the counting and timing take practice.
A foam sleeping pad wrapped around the neck and taped makes a decent soft collar if one is wanted for comfort.
Keep a casualty with a spine injury very well insulated - spinal cord injury can make them lose heat fast.

title: Eye Injuries - Chemicals, Foreign Bodies, and Penetrating Wounds
summary: Flush chemical splashes for at least 15 minutes, remove small specks safely, and shield - never press on or rinse - an eye that has been cut or punctured. Based on Prevent Blindness, AHA-Red Cross 2024 first aid, and CoTCCC guidance.

steps.title: Identify the type of injury
steps.body: Eye injuries fall into a few groups, and the first aid is different for each. Chemical splashes (cleaners, bleach, drain openers, lime, cement, battery acid) need immediate flushing. Small specks such as dust or sand need gentle rinsing. Blows to the eye need cold and a check for serious damage. Cuts, punctures, and anything stuck in the eye need a rigid shield and no rinsing. Ask what happened, and protect your own hands with gloves when possible.

steps.title: Chemical splash: flush right away
steps.body: Every second counts with chemicals - start flushing before you do anything else, including calling for help. Hold the eye open with your fingers and pour or run clean drinking water (or another drinkable liquid if there is no water) from the inner corner near the nose outward, so the runoff does not go into the other eye. A faucet, shower, garden hose on low, or water bottle all work. Flush for at least 15 minutes. If a contact lens is in, start flushing over it; it may wash out.

steps.title: After a chemical splash
steps.body: Do not bandage the eye after flushing. Get emergency care right away, even if the eye feels better, because alkalis such as lye, lime, and cement can keep damaging the eye. Bring the chemical container or label. Call Poison Help at 800-222-1222 for advice on that specific chemical while you arrange care. If you are far from help, keep flushing longer and repeat if pain returns.

steps.title: Specks and small debris
steps.body: Do not rub the eye - rubbing can scratch the clear front surface. Let tears wash the speck out, or rinse gently with clean water or eyewash. Lift the upper lid outward and over the lower lid while the person looks down to help dislodge it. Do not use tweezers, cotton swabs, or other tools on the eye itself. If the speck will not wash out, or the eye stays painful, red, or blurry, see an eye doctor. Protect the eye with a taped shield so the person cannot rub it.

steps.title: Blows to the eye
steps.body: Apply a cold compress gently for about 15 minutes, without pressing on the eyeball. Get emergency care for severe pain, blurred or lost vision, double vision, blood visible inside the colored part of the eye, an eye that sticks out more than the other, or a black eye after a hard blow - these can mean a fracture of the eye socket or bleeding inside the eye.

steps.title: Cuts and penetrating injuries: shield, do not rinse
steps.body: If the eye has been cut or punctured, or something is stuck in it, do not rinse it, do not press on it, and do not try to remove the object. Cover the eye with a rigid shield that rests on the bone around the eye, not on the eye - the bottom of a paper cup, a cut plastic bottle, or a commercial eye shield, taped to the forehead and cheek. If an object sticks out, cut a cup or pad around it so nothing touches it. TCCC also calls for a rigid shield, never a pressure patch. Get emergency care now.

steps.title: Keep the person still and evacuate
steps.body: Keep the person calm and sitting up, with the head still. Ask them not to blow their nose, cough hard, strain, or bend over, which raise pressure in the eye. Covering the uninjured eye too can reduce eye movement, but it can frighten people, so explain first and guide them by the arm. Note how well they can see out of each eye (count fingers, light only, nothing) and write it down. Do not give food or drink if surgery may be needed soon.

warnings: Never press on an injured eye or put a tight pressure patch on a possibly penetrated eye.
Do not try to remove an object stuck in the eye.
Do not bandage an eye after a chemical splash - flush and get care.
proTips: Put a small bottle of eyewash and a rigid eye shield in your kit; a paper cup works in a pinch.
Wear safety glasses when chopping wood, hammering, grinding, or using chemicals - most eye injuries are preventable.
For chemical splashes, a person can lie in the bath or under a shower to make long flushing easier.

title: Impaled Objects and Amputations
summary: Stabilize an object stuck in the body instead of pulling it out, control bleeding from a cut-off limb or finger, and preserve the severed part so surgeons have a chance to reattach it.

steps.title: Call for help and protect yourself
steps.body: Call 911 or send someone for help right away - both injuries need a hospital. Make the scene safe: turn off and lock out machinery, chain saws, or power tools before you reach in. Put on gloves if you have them; otherwise use a plastic bag or several layers of cloth between your hands and the blood. Check the whole person for other injuries and for shock (medical-006).

steps.title: Impaled object: leave it in
steps.body: Do not pull out a knife, stick, rebar, glass, or other object stuck in the body. It may be plugging a torn blood vessel, and removing it can cause sudden heavy bleeding or more damage on the way out. The main exceptions are an object that blocks the airway (such as through the cheek into the mouth) or one that prevents you from giving CPR; even then, remove it only if you must. An object in the eye must also stay put (medical-022).

steps.title: Control bleeding around the object
steps.body: Press firmly around the object, not on it. Pack gauze or clean cloth around the base if the wound is deep. For heavy bleeding from an arm or leg with an impaled object, place a tourniquet 2 to 3 inches above the wound, not over the object (medical-002). Do not push or wiggle the object while you work.

steps.title: Stabilize the object
steps.body: Build up bulky padding around the object - rolled gauze, folded cloth, or rolls of clothing on all sides - so it cannot move. Tape or tie the padding in place. For a long object, a paper cup or ring of rolled cloth placed over the base and taped can help. If the object is too long to move with the person, only trained rescuers with proper tools should cut it, while someone holds it completely still; never try to pull the person off a fixed object such as a fence spike - wait for rescuers unless the scene is about to become deadly.

steps.title: Amputation: stop the bleeding first
steps.body: A fully cut-off limb sometimes bleeds less than expected because the vessels clamp down, but bleeding can start suddenly. For any amputation of a hand, arm, foot, or leg, apply a tourniquet above the stump and tighten until bleeding stops; write down the time. For a finger or toe, firm direct pressure with a clean dressing is usually enough. For a partly cut-off part, keep it in line, cover it, apply only enough pressure to control bleeding, and splint it gently so it does not twist.

steps.title: Save the severed part
steps.body: Find the part if it is safe to do so, but do not delay the person's care to search - it can be brought later. Rinse off dirt gently with clean water without scrubbing. Wrap it in clean gauze or cloth (sources differ on dry or slightly moist - either is acceptable; do not soak it), and seal it in a plastic bag. Put that bag inside another bag or container with ice and water. The part should be cool but must not touch ice directly, sit in water, or freeze. Never use dry ice. Label it with the person's name and the time.

steps.title: Transport together
steps.body: Send the cooled part with the person to the hospital. Reattachment success depends on the part, its condition, and how quickly the person reaches surgery, so move fast. Keep the person lying down and warm, raise the injured limb if possible, and remove rings or watches from the injured limb before swelling. Recheck the tourniquet and dressing after every move.

warnings: Do not remove impaled objects unless they block the airway or prevent CPR.
Do not put a severed part directly on ice, in water, or on dry ice - frozen or waterlogged tissue cannot be reattached.
Never reach into machinery that is still running or could restart.
proTips: Two large zip-top bags and a cooler are a perfect amputated-part kit.
Cut clothing away around an impaled object rather than pulling it over the object.
Tell the hospital ahead of time about the amputation so a hand or limb surgeon can be ready.

title: Wound Cleaning, Closure Options, and Dressing Changes in the Field
summary: Clean a wound with high-pressure drinkable water, decide whether to close it or leave it open, and change dressings while watching for infection when a clinic is far away. Based on Wilderness Medical Society wound guidance.

steps.title: Stop the bleeding and protect yourself
steps.body: Bleeding control always comes first (medical-002, medical-003). Once bleeding is controlled and not life-threatening, you can focus on preventing infection. Wash your hands and wear gloves. Work somewhere as clean and well-lit as you can. Sterile conditions are not required - clean is enough. Remove rings and watches near the wound before swelling starts.

steps.title: Irrigate with plenty of drinkable water
steps.body: Rinsing is the single most important step for preventing infection. Drinkable tap water or properly disinfected water works as well as sterile saline (see water-002 and water-006 for treating water). Use at least 1 quart (1 L) for a small wound and much more for a large or dirty one. Pressure matters: squirt the water hard into the wound using a syringe, a squeeze bottle with a small hole in the cap, or a clean plastic bag with a pinhole poked in one corner. Aim into the wound from a few inches away and let the water run out. Start as soon as practical; earlier is better.

steps.title: Remove debris - skip the harsh antiseptics
steps.body: Pick out loose dirt, gravel, and splinters that come away easily, using tweezers cleaned with boiling water or alcohol. Do not dig deeply. Wash the skin around the wound with soap and water, but do not pour soap, hydrogen peroxide, alcohol, or full-strength iodine into the wound - they damage tissue and slow healing, and the WMS found no proven benefit from adding antiseptics to irrigation water. The exception is a bite from an animal that could carry rabies: scrub it thoroughly with soap and water and get medical care for rabies shots.

steps.title: Decide: close it or leave it open
steps.body: Closing a wound traps germs inside, so be conservative. Leave open: animal and human bites, punctures, gunshot and crush wounds, wounds with dirt you could not fully clean, and wounds more than several hours old. A clean, fresh, straight cut with edges that come together easily can be closed with adhesive strips (butterfly or wound-closure strips) after thorough irrigation. Dry the skin, place strips across the cut every quarter inch or so, and leave small gaps for drainage. Suturing and skin staples are skills for trained people. Gaping wounds, wounds over joints, and face wounds need professional care if possible.

steps.title: Dress open wounds
steps.body: Cover the wound with a nonstick layer (petroleum gauze, a nonstick pad, or a thin layer of petroleum jelly or antibiotic ointment on gauze), then absorbent gauze, then a wrap or tape to hold it. A slightly moist wound heals faster than a dried-out one. Deep open wounds can be loosely filled with moist gauze so they heal from the bottom up - do not pack them tight like a bleeding wound. Splint wounds over joints to reduce movement.

steps.title: Change dressings and inspect daily
steps.body: Change the dressing at least once a day, and any time it gets wet, dirty, or soaked through. Wash your hands, remove the old dressing gently (soak it with clean water if it sticks), rinse the wound again, look at it, and re-dress. Some redness right at the edges and a little clear or pink drainage are normal. Write down what you see each day so you can spot a trend.

steps.title: Watch for infection and know when to evacuate
steps.body: Signs of infection are redness that spreads outward, increasing pain, warmth, swelling, pus or a bad smell, red streaks running up the limb, swollen tender lymph nodes, and fever or chills. If you see these, open any closed wound (remove the strips), irrigate it again, leave it open, and get medical care urgently - antibiotics are a prescription decision. Seek care for any wound that will not stop bleeding, deep wounds of the hand or face, wounds with tendons or bone showing, and any dirty wound if tetanus shots are not current (a booster is usually advised if the last one was more than 5 years ago for dirty wounds).

warnings: Do not close bites, punctures, dirty wounds, or old wounds - they are high infection risk.
Red streaks, fever, or rapidly spreading redness can mean a dangerous infection - get medical care fast.
Do not pour hydrogen peroxide or alcohol into wounds.
proTips: A 1-gallon zip bag with a pinhole is a lightweight high-pressure irrigation system.
Keep your tetanus vaccination up to date before an emergency - it is cheap and easy to get now.
Pack adhesive closure strips and tincture of benzoin (helps strips stick) in your kit.

title: Hypothermia - Mild to Severe
summary: Recognize the stages of hypothermia, stop heat loss, and rewarm safely using the Wilderness Medical Society approach and the 2024 AHA-Red Cross first aid guidelines - including gentle handling and the special CPR rules for very cold patients.

steps.title: Recognize the stage
steps.body: Hypothermia is a core body temperature below 95 F (35 C). In the field you usually judge it by behavior, not a thermometer. Cold stressed: shivering, alert, moving normally - not yet hypothermic. Mild (95 to about 90 F / 35 to 32 C): shivering, clumsy hands, stumbling, poor judgment ('the umbles' - stumbles, mumbles, fumbles). Moderate (about 90 to 82 F / 32 to 28 C): growing confusion, drowsiness, shivering may weaken or stop. Severe (below about 82 F / 28 C): very low responsiveness or unconscious, no shivering, slow weak pulse and breathing; the heart can easily go into a deadly rhythm.

steps.title: Stop further heat loss
steps.body: Get the person out of wind, rain, snow, and water. Get them off the ground - insulation underneath matters as much as on top; use a pad, pack, branches, or extra clothing. Gently remove wet clothing, or cut it off, and replace it with dry layers; if you cannot shelter them, leave damp layers on and wrap over them. Cover the head and neck. Call 911 for anyone who is confused, drowsy, pale or bluish, or has frozen skin.

steps.title: Handle gently and keep them flat
steps.body: In moderate and severe hypothermia, rough handling, sudden movement, and standing or walking can trigger a fatal heart rhythm or collapse ('rescue collapse'). Move the person carefully and keep them lying flat. Do not let a moderate or severe patient walk, and do not rub or massage their arms and legs. Do not put them in a warm shower or bath - that can drop blood pressure and cause collapse.

steps.title: Build a hypothermia wrap
steps.body: Make a 'burrito': lay out a waterproof tarp or plastic sheet, then insulation (sleeping bags, blankets, foam pads). Place the person on top in dry clothing. Add heat sources - hot water bottles wrapped in cloth, or large chemical heat blankets - on the chest, in the armpits, and on the back, never directly on bare skin, which can burn cold skin easily. Wrap the insulation and then a vapor barrier (plastic, emergency blanket, or trash bag) around them, leaving the face clear. Small hand and toe warmers do not deliver enough heat to rewarm a body on their own.

steps.title: Feed and warm the mild patient
steps.body: A person with cold stress or mild hypothermia who is alert and can swallow safely should get high-calorie food and warm, sweet drinks - sugar fuels shivering, which is the body's best heater. Avoid alcohol. Once warm, dry, and fed, a mild patient can do light exercise to generate heat. Mild cases that rewarm fully in the field may not need evacuation, but watch them closely; anyone who stays confused needs care.

steps.title: Evacuate moderate and severe cases
steps.body: Moderate and severe hypothermia need a hospital - some severely cold patients survive only with special rewarming machines. Keep them wrapped, horizontal, and handled gently during transport. Do not give food or drink to anyone who is drowsy or cannot swallow safely. Heat the vehicle or shelter if possible. Keep checking breathing and pulse.

steps.title: CPR rules for very cold patients
steps.body: A severely hypothermic person may have a pulse and breathing so slow they are hard to detect. Check for breathing and a pulse for up to 1 minute. If you find any pulse at all, do not start chest compressions - compressions can trigger cardiac arrest in a cold heart. If there is no pulse or breathing, start CPR (medical-015) and use an AED. Do not assume a cold person is dead just because they look dead; lividity is not a reliable sign. If you must carry a patient during CPR, the WMS allows pausing compressions for up to 5 minutes at a time, then resuming for at least 5 minutes.

warnings: Do not rub frozen or cold limbs and do not use warm showers or baths for moderate or severe hypothermia.
Do not let a moderately or severely hypothermic person stand or walk.
Never place heat packs or hot bottles directly on cold skin - wrap them to prevent burns.
proTips: Carry a lightweight emergency bivy or a large trash bag - it is the vapor barrier for a hypothermia wrap.
Hypothermia happens above freezing: wet, wind, and 40-50 F (4-10 C) weather is classic hypothermia weather.
Check each other for 'the umbles' on cold, wet trips - the person getting hypothermic is usually the last to notice.

title: Frostbite and Non-Freezing Cold Injury (Trench Foot)
summary: Prevent, recognize, and treat frostbite with careful rewarming in warm water - only when refreezing can be prevented - and treat trench (immersion) foot from long exposure to cold, wet conditions. Based on Wilderness Medical Society and 2024 AHA-Red Cross guidance.

steps.title: Recognize frostbite
steps.body: Frostbite is frozen tissue, most often in fingers, toes, nose, ears, and cheeks. Early (frostnip): skin is red or pale, numb, tingling, and returns to normal with warming. Deeper frostbite: skin is white, gray, or waxy, feels hard or wooden, and stays numb. After thawing, blisters may form - clear blisters suggest less deep injury, blood-filled blisters deeper injury. Always check for hypothermia too; if the person is moderately or severely hypothermic, warming the body core comes before treating frostbite (medical-025).

steps.title: Prevent it in the first place
steps.body: Keep skin dry and covered from wind and cold. Wear mittens over gloves, loose boots, and dry socks. Avoid tight clothing and boots, sweating, alcohol, and smoking, which all reduce blood flow. Do not rely on skin creams - they do not protect against frostbite and may raise the risk. Eat and drink enough. Warm any numb or painful finger or toe right away, for example by putting fingers in your armpits or warming feet against a partner's belly.

steps.title: Decide whether to thaw now
steps.body: Refreezing after thawing causes much worse damage than staying frozen. If there is any chance the part will freeze again before you reach safety, keep it frozen and protected, and get to shelter. If walking is the only way out, walking on frozen feet is better than thawing them and then walking. When you can keep the part warm afterward, rewarm it as soon as possible. If immersion is not possible, let it thaw slowly against warm skin or in warm air.

steps.title: Rewarm in warm water
steps.body: Remove rings and tight items. Place the frozen part in clean water at about 99 to 104 F (37 to 40 C) - the 2024 AHA-Red Cross guidance gives this range, and the WMS recommends 98.6 to 102.2 F (37 to 39 C). Use a thermometer if you have one; without one, the water should feel comfortably warm, not hot, to an uninjured hand held in it for 30 seconds. Keep the water at this temperature, adding warm water as it cools. Rewarming usually takes about 30 minutes and is done when the skin is red or purple and soft. Thawing is very painful; over-the-counter ibuprofen (follow the label) may help pain and limit damage, if the person can take it.

steps.title: Protect the thawed tissue
steps.body: Let the skin air-dry or blot it gently. Never rub frostbitten skin, and never rub it with snow. Do not pop or cut blisters. Place bulky, clean, dry gauze or cotton between fingers and toes, and wrap the area loosely to allow for swelling. Aloe vera gel may be applied. Raise the limb above heart level if possible. Do not walk on thawed feet or use thawed hands. Get medical care for any frostbite beyond mild frostnip - early hospital treatment can save fingers and toes.

steps.title: Recognize trench (immersion) foot
steps.body: Trench foot is a non-freezing injury to nerves and blood vessels caused by hours to days in cold, wet conditions, usually below about 59 F (15 C) - wet boots, flooded shelters, or standing in water. Feet become numb, swollen, and pale or blotchy, then cold and clammy; walking can macerate the skin. After rewarming, they often turn red, hot, very painful, and extra sensitive for weeks. Chilblains are a milder version on fingers or shins: itchy, red-purple, swollen patches after repeated damp cold.

steps.title: Treat and prevent trench foot
steps.body: Treat hypothermia or frostbite first. Then remove wet footwear, gently clean and dry the feet, and let them rewarm slowly at room temperature - do not soak them in hot water or massage them. Raise the feet, cover with loose clean dressings, and keep the person off their feet. Get medical care, as pain and nerve damage can last for months. To prevent it, change into dry socks at least daily (more often when wet), dry the feet and air them out, avoid tight boots, and do not sleep in wet socks.

warnings: Do not thaw frostbite if it may refreeze - refreezing causes severe damage.
Never rub frostbitten skin or rub it with snow, and do not use a fire, stove, or heater to thaw it - numb skin burns easily.
Do not use hot water: keep rewarming water at about 99-104 F (37-40 C).
proTips: Carry a spare pair of dry socks in a zip bag, and swap them in at every rest stop on wet trips.
Buddy-check faces for white patches on cold, windy days - you cannot feel frostnip on your own nose.
A cheap aquarium or cooking thermometer in your winter kit makes frostbite rewarming much safer.

title: Heat Exhaustion and Heat Stroke - Cool First
summary: Tell heat exhaustion from heat stroke and cool a heat stroke victim immediately - ideally by cold-water immersion - before and during transport. Based on Wilderness Medical Society heat illness guidance and the EMS 'cool first, transport second' standard.

steps.title: Know the two main heat illnesses
steps.body: Heat exhaustion is the milder form: heavy sweating, thirst, weakness, headache, nausea, dizziness, cramps, and feeling faint, with a normal or only mildly raised temperature and a clear mind. Heat stroke is a life-threatening emergency: the core temperature is above about 104 F (40 C) and the brain is affected. The key difference is mental status. Confusion, strange behavior, slurred speech, stumbling, seizures, or collapse in the heat mean heat stroke until proven otherwise. The skin may be hot and dry or still sweaty - sweating does not rule out heat stroke, especially after exercise.

steps.title: Heat stroke: start cooling immediately
steps.body: Call 911, then start cooling right away - do not wait for EMS or a thermometer. Heat stroke damage depends on how hot the body gets and for how long, so the goal is to bring the temperature down within about 30 minutes. If you suspect heat stroke, treat it as heat stroke. Move the person into shade, remove extra clothing and gear, and protect their airway if they are vomiting or seizing.

steps.title: Cold-water immersion works best
steps.body: Whole-body immersion in cold or ice water is the fastest and preferred method. Use a tub, stock tank, kiddie pool, cooler, creek, or a large tarp or body bag held up at the edges with ice and water poured in (tarp-assisted cooling). Immerse the body up to the neck, keep the head out and supported, and stir or splash the water. Stay with the person every second and keep their face out of the water. Stop cooling when they become clear-minded or, if you can measure it, when the rectal temperature reaches about 101-102 F (38.6-39 C), to avoid overcooling.

steps.title: When you cannot immerse
steps.body: Use the best method you have, and combine them. Drape the person in ice-water-soaked towels or sheets and keep re-wetting them. Spray or pour cool water over the skin while fanning hard - evaporation cooling works about half as well as immersion but is far better than nothing. Cold packs work better on the cheeks, palms, and soles than on the neck, armpits, or groin. Keep cooling during transport. Do not give fever medicines such as acetaminophen or aspirin - they do not help heat stroke.

steps.title: Heat exhaustion: rest, cool, drink
steps.body: Stop all activity and move the person to shade or air conditioning. Have them lie down, loosen or remove extra clothing, and cool the skin with water and fanning. If they are alert and can swallow, give fluids - a sports drink or oral rehydration solution (medical-008) is better than plain water when they have been sweating heavily. Watch them closely. If they get worse, become confused, or do not improve within about 30 minutes, treat them as heat stroke and call 911.

steps.title: Watch for overhydration
steps.body: Drinking huge amounts of plain water during long exertion can dilute the body's salt (exercise-associated hyponatremia), which can also cause confusion, vomiting, swelling, and seizures. The WMS advises drinking to thirst during activity rather than forcing fluids. Someone who is confused after drinking a lot of water needs medical care urgently; do not push more water on them.

steps.title: Prevent heat illness
steps.body: Acclimatize gradually: most heat adaptation happens over about 7 days of 1 to 2 hours of moderate work in the heat. Schedule hard work for cooler hours, take breaks in shade, and wear light, loose clothing. Drink to thirst and eat salty snacks. Watch higher-risk people closely: older adults, young children, people with heart disease, obesity, or a past heat illness, people taking certain medications, and anyone sunburned (sunburn reduces sweating for days). Never leave children or pets in a parked vehicle.

warnings: Confusion or collapse in the heat is heat stroke until proven otherwise - cool first, then transport.
Never leave a person in cooling water unattended; keep the head and airway above water.
Do not give acetaminophen, aspirin, or ibuprofen to treat heat stroke.
proTips: Pre-plan a cooling option at any hot-weather event or work site: a tarp, a cooler of ice water, and towels.
A heavy-duty tarp held up by 3-4 people becomes a cold-water immersion tub anywhere.
Urine color is a quick hydration check - pale yellow is the goal.

title: Drowning and Water Rescue - Reach, Throw, Don't Go
summary: Rescue a struggling swimmer without becoming a second victim, then give CPR with rescue breaths - the 2024 AHA-AAP drowning update stresses breaths, not compressions alone.

steps.title: Recognize drowning
steps.body: Drowning rarely looks like the movies. A drowning person often cannot shout or wave. Look for a head low in the water with the mouth at water level, head tilted back, eyes glassy or closed, upright body with little leg kick, and a ladder-climbing motion with the arms. A child who goes quiet in the water needs checking right away. Shout for help and have someone call 911. Note the spot where you last saw the person, using a landmark on shore.

steps.title: Shout and talk them through it
steps.body: From a safe spot, shout to the person to stay calm and float on their back, arms and legs spread like a starfish, moving their hands gently to stay up. Floating buys time and helps them control their breathing, especially in cold water where the first minute of gasping is the biggest danger. Tell them to grab anything that floats.

steps.title: Reach
steps.body: If the person is close, lie flat or kneel on the bank, dock, or pool edge so you cannot be pulled in, and reach out with a long, sturdy object - a pole, branch, paddle, rope, towel, or piece of clothing. Do not use your bare hand unless you are well anchored. If you start to be pulled in, let go. Pull them in slowly once they grab hold.

steps.title: Throw - and row, but do not go
steps.body: If they are out of reach, throw something that floats: a life ring, life jacket, throw bag, cooler, empty jug with a little water in it for weight, or a ball. With a throw rope, aim past the person so the line falls across them, and keep low as you pull. If a boat is available, row to them and have them hold the boat or an oar - do not use a motor near a person in the water. Do not swim out unless you are trained in water rescue: even strong swimmers drown trying to save someone. Fast or flooded water and ice are especially deadly for rescuers.

steps.title: Get them out and check breathing
steps.body: Once on land or in a boat, lay the person on their back on a firm surface and check responsiveness and breathing for no more than 10 seconds. Anyone pulled from the water who is unresponsive and not breathing normally should be treated as in cardiac arrest. Do not waste time trying to drain water from the lungs or giving abdominal thrusts - that delays oxygen. Neck injury is uncommon unless they dove into shallow water, fell from height, or were in a boat crash.

steps.title: Give CPR with rescue breaths
steps.body: Drowning stops the heart because of lack of oxygen, so breaths matter. The 2024 AHA-AAP update says rescuers should start CPR with both rescue breaths and chest compressions as soon as possible. Give 30 compressions and 2 breaths (medical-015), making sure each breath makes the chest rise. If you are untrained or unable to give breaths, give compressions only until help arrives. Attach an AED as soon as it arrives and dry the chest. Expect vomiting - roll the person to the side, clear the mouth, and continue.

steps.title: Aftercare - everyone goes to the hospital
steps.body: Anyone who needed any rescue breaths or CPR, or who coughed a lot, became confused, or had trouble breathing after a near-drowning, needs a hospital evaluation - lung problems can develop hours later. Remove wet clothing and treat for hypothermia (medical-025). If the person is breathing normally but drowsy, place them in the recovery position and watch them constantly until help arrives.

warnings: Do not enter the water to rescue someone unless you are trained and equipped. Many would-be rescuers drown.
Never walk onto ice to reach someone who has fallen through - reach or throw from shore.
Do not use abdominal thrusts to 'get water out' of a drowning victim - start CPR with breaths.
proTips: Wear a life jacket on boats and near fast water; it is the single best drowning prevention tool.
Keep a throw bag or rope and a life ring where your family swims or near flood-prone areas.
Assign a 'water watcher' at gatherings who does nothing but watch swimmers, without phone or alcohol.

title: Lightning Injuries
summary: Lightning victims are safe to touch and often survive with fast CPR. Learn the 'reverse triage' rule for multiple victims, the injuries to look for, and how to avoid being struck.

steps.title: Make sure you are safe
steps.body: Lightning can strike the same place twice, and a storm that just injured someone is still dangerous. Before helping, check whether you can move the victim and yourself to a safer spot - a hard-roofed building with wiring and plumbing, or a hard-topped vehicle with the windows up. If the storm is still overhead and you must treat in the open, crouch low, stay off ridges and away from tall isolated trees, and work quickly. Call 911 as soon as you can.

steps.title: Victims are safe to touch
steps.body: A person struck by lightning does not carry an electrical charge. You can touch them and start care immediately. This is different from a power-line electrocution, where you must turn off the power first (medical-017). Do not let fear of 'stored electricity' delay CPR.

steps.title: Start CPR immediately if needed
steps.body: Lightning kills by stopping the heart and the breathing. Check each victim for responsiveness and normal breathing. If a victim is not breathing normally, start CPR right away with compressions and rescue breaths (medical-015) and use an AED as soon as one is available. The heart may restart on its own, but breathing can stay stopped longer, so rescue breaths are especially important. Keep going until the person breathes normally, an AED or EMS takes over, or you cannot continue - cardiac arrest is the immediate cause of death in lightning strikes, and prompt CPR is what saves them.

steps.title: Use reverse triage for several victims
steps.body: Normally you help the living first and skip people who appear dead. With lightning, do the opposite: treat the people who are not breathing or have no pulse first. Victims who are moving, groaning, or talking are breathing and will usually survive without immediate help. Those who appear dead may be in a cardiac or breathing arrest that CPR can reverse. Get bystanders to help with CPR and calling 911.

steps.title: Check for other injuries
steps.body: After the immediate threat is handled, look for: burns, often in lines, spots, or fern-like patterns, which may appear hours later; ruptured eardrums and hearing loss; vision problems or temporary blindness; temporary paralysis, where the legs or arms look pale, mottled, and pulseless but usually recover within hours; confusion, memory loss, and head injury; fractures and dislocations from being thrown; and shock from internal injuries. Treat burns (medical-017), splint fractures (medical-018), and keep the person warm and lying down.

steps.title: Everyone struck gets medical care
steps.body: Even if a victim seems fine, lightning can cause hidden heart, nerve, and eye damage. Every person struck, or knocked down by a nearby strike, should be checked by a medical professional. Watch them closely for chest pain, irregular pulse, confusion, or trouble breathing until they reach care. Long-term memory problems, chronic pain, and sleep problems are common after lightning injuries and deserve follow-up.

steps.title: Avoid being struck
steps.body: When thunder roars, go indoors - if you can hear thunder, you are close enough to be struck. Tents, picnic shelters, pavilions, and sheds are not lightning-safe. Only fully enclosed buildings with wiring and plumbing, or a hard-topped vehicle with windows closed, protect you. Wait 30 minutes after the last thunder before going back out, and restart the count with each new rumble. If caught outdoors, get off peaks and ridges, away from water and metal fences, and spread a group out at least several yards apart so one strike does not hit everyone.

warnings: Do not delay CPR - lightning victims carry no charge and are safe to touch.
Do not use normal triage with lightning - treat those who appear dead first.
Shelters without walls, tents, and trees do not protect you from lightning.
proTips: Plan hikes and outdoor work to be off exposed terrain by early afternoon in thunderstorm season.
Teach your group the 30-minute rule before the trip, not during the storm.
Keep a phone-based or radio weather alert on during outdoor events.

title: Crush Injuries and People Trapped in Collapsed Buildings
summary: Help a person pinned under debris or a heavy object without endangering yourself, prepare for the dangers that come with release (crush syndrome), and know what trained rescuers and medics will do. Based on the 2025 FPHC crush injury consensus and CoTCCC guidance.

steps.title: Size up the scene before you go in
steps.body: Collapsed buildings kill rescuers through secondary collapse, gas leaks, fire, electricity, and falling debris. Do not enter a badly damaged structure unless you are trained, equipped, and the risk is clearly worth it. Shut off gas and electricity if you can do so safely. Call 911 or local rescue and report the exact location, number of trapped people, and what is pinning them. Work in pairs, wear gloves, sturdy boots, a helmet or hard hat, and a dust mask, and know your way out. See dis-003 for earthquake safety.

steps.title: Make contact and assess
steps.body: Call out and listen for voices or tapping. When you reach someone, talk to them: their name, where they hurt, what is on top of them, whether they can feel and move their limbs, and how long they have been trapped. Check breathing and look for heavy bleeding. Clear dust from the mouth and nose and give them a dust mask or cloth to breathe through. Reassure them; trapped people panic easily, and panic makes rescue harder.

steps.title: Treat what you can reach
steps.body: Stop any life-threatening bleeding you can reach with a tourniquet, packing, or pressure (medical-002, medical-003). Open and protect the airway. Keep the person warm with blankets, as trapped people lose heat to rubble and the ground. If they are alert, can swallow, and rescue will take a long time, small sips of water are reasonable. Note the time you found them and the time the compression began, if known.

steps.title: Understand crush syndrome
steps.body: When a large muscle mass (such as a thigh, hips, or both legs) is crushed for a long time, the muscle cells die and release potassium, acids, and muscle proteins. While the weight is on, these toxins stay trapped. When the weight is lifted, they can rush into the bloodstream and cause a sudden dangerous heart rhythm, shock, or kidney failure - sometimes minutes after a person who seemed fine is freed. The longer and heavier the compression, the higher the risk.

steps.title: Free them as soon as it is safe
steps.body: The 2025 FPHC consensus says the earliest safe release of the crushing force is a top priority, because time under compression is the main risk factor you can change. Do not leave someone trapped just to 'wait for fluids.' Lift loads with levers, jacks, or cribbing (wood blocks placed under the load as it rises so it cannot drop back), not by hand alone. Coordinate with rescue teams if they are on scene. Before release, it is sensible to place a tourniquet loosely around a badly crushed limb, as high as needed, ready to tighten if heavy bleeding starts after release.

steps.title: What trained medics will do
steps.body: If paramedics or medics are available, they may give IV fluids before or during release, as long as this does not delay getting the person out, and monitor the heart for changes caused by high potassium. These treatments, and medicines for high potassium, are prescription and protocol-based - do not attempt them yourself. Tourniquets are not routinely used to prevent crush syndrome; they are for heavy bleeding. Amputation to free someone is a last resort for trained surgeons only, when the person's life is about to be lost.

steps.title: After release - watch and evacuate
steps.body: Treat the freed person as a seriously injured trauma patient even if they look well. Lay them flat, keep them warm, splint crushed limbs, and watch breathing, pulse, and alertness constantly. Sudden collapse, an irregular pulse, very dark (cola-colored) urine, little or no urine, or rapidly swelling, rock-hard, painful limbs are emergencies. Anyone trapped under significant weight for more than a short time needs hospital care, ideally a trauma center, as fast as possible.

warnings: Do not enter an unstable collapsed structure without training and equipment - rescuers die in secondary collapses.
A trapped person who seems fine can collapse suddenly after release. Be ready for CPR (medical-015).
Never lift a heavy load without cribbing beneath it; a dropped load can kill the victim or rescuer.
proTips: Take a CERT (Community Emergency Response Team) class to learn light search and rescue, cribbing, and leverage safely.
Keep a whistle, gloves, dust masks, a pry bar, and a flashlight in your home disaster kit.
Mark searched areas with chalk or tape so other rescuers do not repeat your work.

title: Patient Assessment Without Equipment
summary: A repeatable head-to-toe system for any sick or injured person: scene safety, primary survey for life threats, vital signs with just a watch, a SAMPLE history, and a clear handoff report. Modeled on the NREMT assessment sequence and TCCC.

steps.title: Scene size-up
steps.body: Before you touch anyone, stop and look. Is the scene safe from traffic, fire, electricity, water, falling objects, weapons, or toxic gas? Put on gloves if you have them. Figure out what happened (a fall, crash, illness), how many people are hurt, and whether you need more help - call 911 or send someone now, not later. Consider whether the mechanism could have hurt the spine. If the scene is not safe and you cannot make it safe, do not go in.

steps.title: First impression and responsiveness
steps.body: As you approach, form a quick impression: does the person look very sick or not? Then check responsiveness with AVPU. A - Alert: eyes open, talking. V - responds to Voice. P - responds only to Pain (a firm pinch on the shoulder muscle). U - Unresponsive. If they are unresponsive and not breathing normally, start CPR right away (medical-015). Introduce yourself to a conscious person and ask permission to help.

steps.title: Primary survey - find and fix life threats
steps.body: Work quickly through the threats that kill fastest, fixing each as you find it. For injuries use MARCH (medical-001): Massive bleeding - look and sweep your hands over the body, including under the person; stop heavy bleeding now. Airway - is it open and clear? Respiration - is breathing present, normal, and easy? Look for chest wounds. Circulation - check the pulse at the wrist, skin color and temperature, and signs of shock. Hypothermia/Head - keep them warm and note alertness. This survey should take about a minute. Decide now whether this person needs urgent evacuation.

steps.title: Vital signs with just a watch
steps.body: Pulse: feel the thumb side of the wrist (or the side of the neck) and count beats for 30 seconds, then double it. Normal adult resting rate is about 60 to 100. Breathing: watch the chest rise for 30 seconds and double it; normal adult rate is about 12 to 20, quiet and easy. Skin: note color (pink, pale, gray, blue), temperature (warm, cool), and moisture (dry, sweaty). Alertness: AVPU, plus whether they know their name, place, and what happened. Pupils: equal, and both shrink in light? Write each set down with the time and repeat every 5 to 15 minutes.

steps.title: SAMPLE history
steps.body: Ask the person, or bystanders and family, these questions. S - Signs and symptoms: what hurts or feels wrong? For pain, ask when it started, what makes it better or worse, what it feels like, where it goes, and how bad it is from 0 to 10. A - Allergies to medicines, foods, or stings. M - Medications, including blood thinners, insulin, and inhalers; look for medical ID bracelets. P - Past medical history: heart, lung, diabetes, seizures, pregnancy. L - Last oral intake (food and drink) and last urination. E - Events leading up to the illness or injury.

steps.title: Head-to-toe secondary check
steps.body: When life threats are handled, check the whole body in order: head and face, neck, chest, belly, pelvis, back, each arm and leg. Look for wounds, bruising, swelling, and deformity; gently feel for tenderness; ask about pain at each area. Press gently on the pelvis only once - if it is painful or unstable, stop and do not rock it. Check feeling, movement, and circulation in each hand and foot. Expose areas you need to see, then cover the person again to keep them warm and protect their privacy.

steps.title: Keep reassessing
steps.body: A patient's condition changes. Repeat the primary survey and vital signs every 5 minutes for anyone seriously hurt or ill, and every 15 minutes for someone stable, plus after every move or treatment. Compare each set to the last: a rising pulse, faster breathing, cooler skin, or falling alertness means things are getting worse. Keep a written log; if you are caring for several people, use tape or a card on each person.

steps.title: Give a clear handoff report
steps.body: When EMS or another caregiver takes over, give a short, organized report. For trauma, use MIST: Mechanism (what happened and when), Injuries found, Signs (vital signs and trends), and Treatments given with times (tourniquet time, medicines, positioning). For illness, give age, chief complaint, the SAMPLE history, vital signs and trends, and what you did. Hand over your written notes and any medicine containers. Stay until the new caregiver has what they need.

warnings: Never let the assessment delay treatment of a life threat - fix heavy bleeding or a blocked airway the moment you find it.
Do not move someone with a possible spine injury just to examine them.
A normal first set of vital signs does not mean the person is safe. Repeat them.
proTips: Practice taking pulse and breathing rates on family members to learn what normal feels like.
Carry a pencil and a small waterproof notebook or a strip of duct tape and a marker in your kit for notes.
Ask open questions ('Tell me what happened') before yes/no questions - you learn more.

title: Heart Attack - Recognition and What to Do
summary: Recognize the warning signs of a heart attack, call 911 fast, consider chewing aspirin per current AHA/Red Cross first aid guidance, and be ready for CPR.

steps.title: Know the warning signs
steps.body: The American Heart Association lists these signs: discomfort in the center of the chest lasting more than a few minutes or that goes away and comes back - often pressure, squeezing, fullness, or pain; pain or discomfort in one or both arms, the back, neck, jaw, or stomach; shortness of breath with or without chest discomfort; and other signs such as a cold sweat, nausea, or lightheadedness. Symptoms can be mild and build slowly. Some people, especially women, older adults, and people with diabetes, may have shortness of breath, nausea, or unusual tiredness without strong chest pain.

steps.title: Call 911 right away
steps.body: Do not wait to see if it passes, and do not drive the person yourself if EMS is available - paramedics can start treatment and send heart tracings to the hospital on the way. Tell the dispatcher you suspect a heart attack and follow their instructions. Note the time symptoms started. Unlock the door, turn on outside lights, and send someone to meet the ambulance. If help truly cannot come, plan the fastest transport to a hospital while following the steps below.

steps.title: Rest and position
steps.body: Have the person stop all activity and sit or lie in whatever position is most comfortable, often sitting up with knees bent and back supported. Loosen tight clothing. Keep them calm and warm. Do not let them walk around, climb stairs, or carry anything. Exertion makes the heart work harder and can worsen damage.

steps.title: Consider aspirin
steps.body: The 2024 AHA and American Red Cross first aid guidelines say that while waiting for EMS, an alert adult with chest pain not caused by injury may be encouraged to chew and swallow 162-325 mg of aspirin - for example, two to four 81 mg low-dose tablets or one 325 mg regular tablet. Chewing works faster than swallowing whole. Do not give aspirin if the person is allergic to it, has been told by a clinician not to take it, is not fully alert, or cannot swallow. If you are unsure, it is reasonable to skip aspirin and wait for EMS. Never delay calling 911 to find aspirin.

steps.title: Help with their own medicines
steps.body: If the person has been prescribed nitroglycerin for chest pain, help them take it exactly as their doctor and label instruct. Do not give anyone else's prescription medicine. Gather their medication list, allergies, and medical history for EMS. Stay with them and watch breathing and responsiveness closely.

steps.title: Be ready for cardiac arrest
steps.body: A heart attack can turn into cardiac arrest without warning. If the person stops responding and is not breathing normally - or is only gasping - shout for help, call 911 if not already done, and start hands-only CPR: push hard and fast in the center of the chest, about 2 inches (5 cm) deep, at 100-120 compressions per minute. Send someone for an AED and use it as soon as it arrives, following the voice prompts.

steps.title: After the episode
steps.body: Even if symptoms fade, the person needs emergency evaluation the same day - heart damage can continue silently. In a grid-down situation with no hospital, keep the person resting, sitting up, warm, and hydrated with small sips, and arrange evacuation to any facility with a doctor as soon as possible. Record times, symptoms, and anything given.

warnings: Never give aspirin to someone allergic to it, told not to take it, not fully alert, or unable to swallow.
Do not let the person drive themselves or walk to help.
Do not delay calling 911 to see if symptoms pass.
Chest pain after an injury is not a reason for aspirin - it may increase bleeding.
proTips: Keep a bottle of 81 mg chewable aspirin in your car and home first aid kits.
Learn hands-only CPR and where the nearest AED is at home, work, and church.
Write each family member's medications and allergies on a card in your wallet or phone.
Note the time symptoms started - hospitals use it for treatment decisions.
source: AHA / American Red Cross First Aid Guidelines 2024

immediate: Call 911 and note the time symptoms started

title: Stroke - BE FAST and Time of Onset
summary: Spot a stroke with BE FAST (Balance, Eyes, Face, Arms, Speech, Time), call 911 immediately, and record when the person was last known well - treatment depends on it.

steps.title: Know the sudden signs
steps.body: Stroke signs come on suddenly. CDC lists sudden numbness or weakness of the face, arm, or leg, especially on one side; sudden confusion, trouble speaking, or trouble understanding; sudden trouble seeing in one or both eyes; sudden trouble walking, dizziness, or loss of balance; and sudden severe headache with no known cause. The key word is sudden. A person may not realize anything is wrong, so trust what you see.

steps.title: Run the BE FAST check
steps.body: B - Balance: is the person suddenly dizzy, unsteady, or uncoordinated? E - Eyes: sudden blurred, double, or lost vision? F - Face: ask them to smile; does one side droop? A - Arms: ask them to raise both arms; does one drift down or feel weak? S - Speech: ask them to repeat a simple sentence like 'The sky is blue'; is it slurred, strange, or impossible? T - Time: if you see any of these signs, call 911 now. The 2024 AHA/Red Cross first aid guidelines recommend using a stroke scale like FAST for adults.

steps.title: Call 911 - do not drive
steps.body: Call 911 even if the signs seem mild or start to go away. CDC advises against driving yourself or having a family member drive, because EMS can start care, check blood sugar, and alert the stroke team so treatment begins the moment you arrive. Brain cells die quickly when blood flow stops; every minute counts. Say 'possible stroke' to the dispatcher.

steps.title: Write down the time
steps.body: Record when symptoms started, or the last time the person was seen normal (for example, 'went to bed fine at 10 p.m.'). The best clot-busting treatments only work within a few hours of onset - CDC notes the most effective treatments require diagnosis within about 3 hours of the first symptoms. If you are not sure, give the last known well time; do not guess the onset. Also note medicines, especially blood thinners.

steps.title: Keep them safe while waiting
steps.body: Keep the person still and comfortable. If they are alert, let them sit or lie with head and shoulders slightly raised. If they are drowsy but breathing normally, place them on their side in the recovery position so saliva or vomit drains. Give nothing to eat or drink - stroke can affect swallowing and cause choking. Do not give aspirin; some strokes are caused by bleeding in the brain.

steps.title: Check blood sugar if you can
steps.body: Very low blood sugar can look exactly like a stroke. The AHA guidelines say checking blood glucose is reasonable if a meter is available and it does not delay calling EMS. If the reading is low and the person is fully alert and can swallow, follow guide medical-045, but still get emergency evaluation.

steps.title: Treat a TIA as an emergency
steps.body: If symptoms go away within minutes, it may be a transient ischemic attack (TIA, or 'mini-stroke'). This is a warning that a larger stroke may follow soon. The person still needs emergency evaluation right away. In a grid-down situation, arrange the fastest possible transport to a hospital and keep a written record of signs and times.

warnings: Never give food, drink, or aspirin to a suspected stroke patient.
Do not wait to see if symptoms pass - call 911 at once.
Adult stroke scales are not reliable in children; a child with sudden weakness, confusion, or speech change needs EMS regardless.
If the person becomes unresponsive and stops breathing normally, start CPR.
proTips: Teach every family member BE FAST, including kids.
Use your phone clock or a photo timestamp to fix the onset time.
Bring the person's medication list and ID to the hospital or hand it to EMS.
A glucose meter in the family kit helps rule out low sugar mimics.

Do not let a negative FAST check reassure you if other sudden neurologic signs are present.

immediate: Check BE FAST: Balance, Eyes, Face, Arms, Speech
Call 911 now - do not drive them yourself
Write down the time symptoms started or last known well
then: Nothing by mouth; recovery position if drowsy
