title: Anaphylaxis and Epinephrine Auto-Injectors
summary: Recognize a severe allergic reaction fast, use the person's epinephrine auto-injector or nasal spray following the device instructions, call 911, and know when a second dose may be needed.

steps.title: Recognize anaphylaxis
steps.body: Anaphylaxis is a fast, body-wide allergic reaction, often within minutes of a food, sting, medicine, or latex exposure. Warning signs include swelling of the lips, tongue, or face; a feeling that the throat is closing; hoarse voice; trouble breathing or wheezing; widespread hives or itching; vomiting, cramps, or diarrhea; and signs of low blood pressure such as dizziness, pale or clammy skin, fainting, or confusion. Two or more body systems involved, or any breathing or circulation problem after a known trigger, should be treated as anaphylaxis.

steps.title: Give epinephrine first - when in doubt, give it
steps.body: Epinephrine is the only first-line treatment. AHA/Red Cross 2024 first aid guidelines say the person should use their own auto-injector, and a first aid provider should help if needed. Allergy experts advise giving epinephrine even if you are unsure the reaction is severe enough; the harm of waiting is far greater than the harm of an unneeded dose. Antihistamines like diphenhydramine are too slow and do not replace epinephrine.

steps.title: Use the device exactly as labeled
steps.body: Read the instructions printed on the device - each brand differs. For most auto-injectors: remove the safety cap, hold the tip against the middle of the outer thigh (it can go through clothing), press firmly until it clicks, and hold it in place for the time stated on the label. Never put a thumb over the tip. The FDA approved neffy, an epinephrine nasal spray, in 2024 for people who weigh at least 66 lb (30 kg), and in 2025 a lower-strength version for children who weigh about 33 to 66 lb (15 to 30 kg); spray it in one nostril as the package directs. If a second dose is needed, the label allows it 5 minutes after the first.

steps.title: Call 911 immediately
steps.body: Call 911 or have someone call as you give the epinephrine. Anaphylaxis can come back after the medicine wears off, so the person needs emergency care and monitoring even if they feel better. Tell the dispatcher it is anaphylaxis and that epinephrine was given, and note the time. Give the used device to EMS.

steps.title: Position the person
steps.body: If they are having trouble breathing, let them sit up in the position that is easiest. If they feel faint or dizzy, have them lie flat, and raise their legs if that is comfortable. Do not have them stand or walk suddenly - blood pressure can crash. If they vomit or become drowsy while breathing, roll them onto their side. Loosen tight clothing and keep them warm.

steps.title: Watch for a second dose
steps.body: The 2024 guidelines say a repeat dose may be considered if there is no response to the first dose and EMS is more than 5-10 minutes away. Use a new device and follow its label; for neffy, the FDA label says to use a new spray in the same nostril if symptoms do not improve or get worse. Many people with allergies carry two devices for this reason.

steps.title: Start CPR if needed and follow up
steps.body: If the person becomes unresponsive and is not breathing normally, start CPR and use an AED if available. After any anaphylaxis, the person should be seen by a clinician and referred to an allergist, get a written action plan, and replace used devices. Check expiration dates and keep devices out of extreme heat and cold.

warnings: Do not wait for symptoms to get worse before giving epinephrine.
Antihistamines and inhalers do not replace epinephrine in anaphylaxis.
Do not stand a person with anaphylaxis upright suddenly - they can collapse.
Always call 911 after using epinephrine, even if the person improves.
proTips: Carry two doses - a second dose is sometimes needed before EMS arrives.
Practice with a trainer device so your hands know the steps under stress.
Store devices at room temperature in an insulated pouch; heat and freezing damage them.
Teach children and caregivers where the device is kept and how to use it.

Do not inject into a vein, buttock, hand, or foot - use the outer thigh as the device directs.

immediate: Give their epinephrine auto-injector or nasal spray per the device instructions

Start CPR if they stop breathing normally

title: Asthma Attack Without a Nebulizer
summary: Help someone through an asthma attack using their own quick-relief inhaler and a spacer - commercial or improvised - and know the danger signs that mean 911 now.

steps.title: Recognize an attack
steps.body: Common signs are coughing, wheezing, chest tightness, and shortness of breath. Worsening signs are fast, labored breathing, the skin pulling in between the ribs or above the collarbone with each breath, flaring nostrils, and a quick-relief inhaler that is not helping. Emergency signs include blue or gray lips or fingernails, being unable to speak in full sentences or walk, confusion or drowsiness, and a chest that has gone quiet because very little air is moving.

steps.title: Stay calm and sit them up
steps.body: Have the person sit upright, leaning slightly forward with hands on knees or a table - whatever position is easiest. Do not lay them flat. Loosen tight clothing. Speak calmly and coach slow breathing; panic tightens the airways and speeds breathing. Move them away from smoke, dust, pets, cold air, or other triggers if you can do so quickly.

steps.title: Use their quick-relief inhaler
steps.body: The 2024 AHA/Red Cross first aid guidelines say a first aid provider should help a person use their own prescribed bronchodilator. Follow the person's asthma action plan or the inhaler label for the number of puffs and timing. Shake the inhaler, remove the cap, and check the counter if it has one. If they have never used it before or are too breathless to coordinate, a spacer makes a big difference.

steps.title: Use a spacer - or make one
steps.body: The guidelines say an inhaler with a spacer works better than an inhaler alone, and an improvised spacer is reasonable when no commercial one is available. To improvise, cut a hole in the bottom of a clean 16-20 oz (500 ml) plastic bottle just big enough for the inhaler mouthpiece, seal around it with tape, and have the person breathe from the bottle's open neck. Fire one puff into the bottle and have them take 4-6 slow breaths in and out before the next puff. A rolled paper tube or a paper cup with a hole works in a pinch.

steps.title: Reassess every few minutes
steps.body: Check whether breathing is getting easier, speech is improving, and color is normal. If there is no clear improvement within about 20 minutes, or the person is getting worse at any point, call 911 or get them to emergency care. Keep the inhaler and spacer going as their action plan directs while you wait.

steps.title: Call 911 for danger signs
steps.body: Call 911 immediately for blue or gray lips or nails, inability to speak or walk, severe retractions, drowsiness or confusion, or no response to the inhaler. If the attack follows a food, sting, or medicine exposure with hives or swelling, treat it as anaphylaxis and use epinephrine if available (see medical-042). If the person becomes unresponsive and stops breathing normally, start CPR.

steps.title: After the attack
steps.body: Even a resolved attack needs follow-up with a clinician, especially if the inhaler was needed more than usual. Note what triggered it, how many puffs were used, and how long recovery took. In a grid-down situation, reduce triggers: no indoor smoke, filter or ventilate air, keep bedding dust-free, and ration inhalers carefully while seeking a refill.

warnings: Do not lay a person having an asthma attack flat on their back.
Blue lips, inability to speak, or a 'quiet chest' are emergencies - call 911.
Do not use someone else's prescription inhaler unless directed by a dispatcher or clinician in an emergency.
Wheezing with hives, swelling, or vomiting after an exposure may be anaphylaxis - use epinephrine.
proTips: Keep a spare inhaler and a collapsible spacer in your bug-out bag and car.
Check inhaler expiration dates and dose counters every month.
Practice making a bottle spacer once so you can do it fast in the dark.
Indoor generators, wood stoves with poor draft, and candles are common grid-down triggers.
source: AHA-American Red Cross First Aid 2024 / Rady Children's Hospital

Do not use an improvised spacer instead of a commercial one if a commercial spacer is available.

immediate: Sit them upright, leaning forward; keep calm
Help them use their quick-relief inhaler per their action plan
Use a spacer - improvise with a plastic bottle if needed

title: Seizures - Protect, Time, Recover
summary: Keep a person safe during a seizure, time it, roll them onto their side, and know exactly when a seizure becomes a 911 emergency.

steps.title: Stay calm and start timing
steps.body: Most seizures stop on their own within a few minutes. Note the time it started - use your phone clock - because duration decides whether to call 911. Stay with the person the whole time and keep bystanders calm and back. Look for a medical ID bracelet or card that lists epilepsy, diabetes, or emergency contacts.

steps.title: Protect from injury
steps.body: If they are falling, ease them to the ground. Move hard or sharp objects, furniture, and hot items away. Cushion the head with something soft and flat like a folded jacket. Remove eyeglasses and loosen anything tight around the neck. If they are near water, a road, stairs, or a fire, protect them from it; move them only if they are in immediate danger.

steps.title: Do not restrain, do not put anything in the mouth
steps.body: Do not hold the person down or try to stop the movements - that can injure both of you. Never put anything in their mouth, including fingers, spoons, or a wallet; a person cannot swallow their tongue, and objects can break teeth or block the airway. Do not give rescue breaths during the seizure; breathing usually restarts on its own when the seizure ends.

steps.title: Roll them onto their side
steps.body: As soon as it is safe - during or right after the jerking - gently roll the person onto their side so saliva and vomit can drain and the airway stays open. Bend the top knee forward to keep them from rolling back. Stay beside them and watch their breathing and color.

steps.title: Know when to call 911
steps.body: The 2024 AHA/Red Cross first aid guidelines and CDC say to call 911 if: it is the person's first seizure; it lasts longer than 5 minutes; another seizure follows without them waking up in between; they have trouble breathing or do not wake up; they are injured; the seizure happened in water; they are pregnant; they have diabetes; it happens in an infant under 6 months; or they do not return to their usual self within 5-10 minutes after the shaking stops.

steps.title: Help them recover
steps.body: After the seizure, people are often confused, sleepy, embarrassed, or scared for a while. Speak softly, tell them where they are and what happened, and keep onlookers away. Do not give food, drink, or pills until they are fully awake and can swallow normally. Help them to a safe place to rest, and arrange for someone to stay with them or get them home.

steps.title: Record and follow up
steps.body: Write down when it started and stopped, what the movements looked like, which side of the body was involved, whether they lost bladder control or bit their tongue, and how long recovery took. This helps their doctor. Seizures can be caused by fever in young children, head injury, low blood sugar, heat illness, alcohol or drug withdrawal, or poisoning - look for and treat a cause when you can.

warnings: Never put anything in a seizing person's mouth.
Do not hold the person down.
A seizure lasting over 5 minutes, or back-to-back seizures, is an emergency - call 911.
Give nothing by mouth until the person is fully alert.

If the person has a seizure action plan or rescue medicine prescribed, follow that plan.
A seizure in a diabetic may be low blood sugar - see medical-045 once they are awake.
Some seizures are just staring or confusion; stay with the person and guide them away from danger.

title: Diabetic Emergencies - Low and High Blood Sugar
summary: Treat low blood sugar quickly with fast sugar using the 15-15 rule, recognize the slower danger of very high sugar and ketoacidosis, and know when to call 911.

steps.title: Spot low blood sugar
steps.body: Low blood sugar (hypoglycemia, usually under 70 mg/dL) can come on in minutes, especially in people who take insulin or certain diabetes pills, skip meals, or exercise hard. Signs include shakiness, sweating, fast heartbeat, hunger, irritability, pale skin, headache, confusion or 'brain fog', slurred speech, clumsiness, and odd behavior that can look like drunkenness or a stroke. Severe lows cause seizures or unconsciousness. If you are unsure whether sugar is low or high and the person is awake, treat as low - sugar will not hurt much in the short term.

steps.title: Give fast sugar if they can swallow
steps.body: The 2024 AHA/Red Cross first aid guidelines say to encourage oral glucose if the person is awake and able to swallow. Glucose tablets are preferred over gel or food; if none are available, use simple sugars. CDC lists examples of about 15 grams of carbohydrate: 3-4 glucose tablets, one tube of glucose gel, 4 oz (1/2 cup, 120 ml) of juice or regular (not diet) soda, or 1 tablespoon of sugar, honey, or syrup. Young children may need less. Avoid chocolate or fatty foods for the first dose - fat slows sugar absorption.

steps.title: Follow the 15-15 rule
steps.body: After 15 grams of carbohydrate, wait 15 minutes and recheck blood sugar if a meter is available. If it is still under 70 mg/dL or symptoms remain, give another 15 grams. Repeat until it is back in range. Once the person feels better, give a snack or meal with protein and starch, such as crackers with cheese or peanut butter, to keep it from dropping again.

steps.title: Call 911 when needed
steps.body: Never put food or drink in the mouth of someone who is not fully awake or cannot swallow - it can cause choking. Call 911 if the person cannot swallow, has a seizure, is unconscious, or does not improve within about 10 minutes of oral glucose. If they become unresponsive, place them on their side if they are breathing normally and watch them closely; start CPR if they are not breathing normally.

steps.title: Use prescribed glucagon if available
steps.body: Glucagon is a prescription emergency medicine for severe lows, available as an injection or nasal powder. If the person has one and you have been shown how, use it exactly as the package directs, then call 911. CDC notes people usually wake within about 15 minutes; once awake and able to swallow, give fast sugar and then a longer-acting snack. Always get emergency care after glucagon is used.

steps.title: Recognize dangerously high blood sugar
steps.body: High blood sugar builds more slowly over hours to days, often from missed insulin, a failed pump, illness, or infection. Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) is a life-threatening result. Signs include intense thirst, frequent urination, nausea, vomiting, belly pain, weakness, fruity-smelling breath, fast deep breathing, and confusion. Mayo Clinic advises emergency care for blood sugar above 300 mg/dL (16.7 mmol/L) on more than one check, ketones in the urine with no way to reach a clinician, or several DKA signs at once.

steps.title: Plan for grid-down diabetes
steps.body: Keep at least a two-week supply of medicines, test strips, glucose tablets, and ketone strips. Insulin should be kept cool but never frozen; follow the label for room-temperature limits. Encourage people with diabetes to keep drinking water during illness, check sugar more often, and follow the sick-day plan from their care team. Vomiting with high sugar or ketones means emergency care - IV fluids and insulin cannot be replaced in the field.

warnings: Never give food, drink, or glucose by mouth to someone who is not fully awake or cannot swallow.
Do not give insulin to someone with suspected low blood sugar.
Vomiting, fruity breath, fast breathing, and confusion with high sugar may be DKA - get emergency care.
Low sugar can mimic drunkenness or stroke - check before assuming.
proTips: Keep glucose tablets in every kit, glovebox, and backpack - they do not melt or spoil easily.
Teach family members where the glucagon is and how to use it.
For an awake child who will not swallow, a sugar-and-water paste under the tongue may help per AHA guidance while you call 911.
Write the person's diabetes medicines and doses on a card for EMS.

title: Poisoning and Overdose - Poison Control and Naloxone
summary: Respond to swallowed, skin, eye, and inhaled poisonings, call Poison Help at 1-800-222-1222 or 911, and use over-the-counter naloxone for a suspected opioid overdose.

steps.title: Decide: 911 or Poison Help
steps.body: Call 911 right away if the person is drowsy or unconscious, has trouble breathing or has stopped breathing, is having a seizure, is uncontrollably agitated, or is known to have taken an overdose. If the person is awake and stable with no symptoms, call Poison Help at 1-800-222-1222. It is free, confidential, and answered 24/7 by poison specialists anywhere in the U.S. They will tell you whether home care is safe or a hospital visit is needed.

steps.title: Have the facts ready
steps.body: Poison specialists and EMS need the person's age and weight, the product or medicine (bring the container or label), how much was taken, when it happened, how it entered the body, current symptoms, and any other medicines or conditions. Save pill bottles, packaging, plant parts, or a photo of the mushroom or substance. Do not wait for symptoms to call - many poisons, including acetaminophen, look harmless for hours before serious damage shows.

steps.title: First aid by route
steps.body: Swallowed: remove anything left in the mouth; follow the product label's poisoning directions while you call. On skin: put on gloves, remove contaminated clothing, and rinse skin under running water for 15-20 minutes. In the eye: flush gently with lukewarm or cool water for about 20 minutes. Inhaled gas or fumes: get the person to fresh air if you can do so without exposing yourself. If the person vomits, turn their head or body to the side.

steps.title: Do not make them vomit
steps.body: Do not give syrup of ipecac, salt water, or fingers down the throat. Expert groups no longer recommend inducing vomiting; it can cause more harm, especially with corrosive or petroleum products. Do not give milk, water, charcoal, or any 'antidote' unless Poison Help or EMS tells you to. Discard any old ipecac in your kit.

steps.title: Recognize an opioid overdose
steps.body: Opioid overdose - from pain pills, heroin, or fentanyl, including fentanyl hidden in other drugs - causes very slow or stopped breathing, gurgling or snoring sounds, tiny pupils, blue or gray lips and fingertips, limpness, and no response to shouting or a firm sternum rub. It can happen to someone taking a prescribed medicine or a child who finds pills or a patch.

steps.title: Give naloxone and support breathing
steps.body: The FDA approved Narcan 4 mg nasal spray for sale without a prescription in March 2023. Follow the package instructions: lay the person on their back, insert the nozzle in a nostril, and press the plunger fully. AHA/Red Cross 2024 guidelines say for an unresponsive person who is not breathing normally, call 911, start CPR with compressions and breaths, and give naloxone. If there is no response in a few minutes, give another dose in the other nostril per the package. When breathing returns, place them on their side.

steps.title: Stay until help arrives
steps.body: Naloxone can wear off before the opioid does, so breathing can stop again - stay with the person and watch them until EMS takes over. They may wake up confused, sick, or in withdrawal (body aches, vomiting, sweating); keep them calm and on their side. Check children for medicated patches on the skin or in the mouth and remove them. A swallowed button battery or magnet needs an emergency X-ray right away.

warnings: Never induce vomiting unless Poison Help or a clinician tells you to.
Protect yourself - do not enter a space with gas or fumes, and wear gloves for chemical spills.
Naloxone wears off; always call 911 and stay with the person.
Swallowed button batteries can burn through the esophagus within hours - go to the ER immediately.
proTips: Save 1-800-222-1222 in every family phone and post it inside a kitchen cabinet.
Keep naloxone in your home, car, and bug-out kit - it is OTC and has no effect on someone who has not taken opioids.
Store medicines and chemicals locked, up high, and in original labeled containers.
In a grid-down situation, label every repackaged fuel or chemical clearly - mix-ups cause poisonings.

title: Carbon Monoxide Poisoning - Symptoms and Response
summary: Carbon monoxide is an invisible, odorless gas that kills quickly during power outages. Recognize the symptoms, get everyone into fresh air, call 911, and prevent it with alarms and safe generator use.

steps.title: Know where CO comes from
steps.body: Carbon monoxide (CO) is made whenever fuel burns: generators, gas or charcoal grills, camp stoves, kerosene and propane heaters, wood stoves and fireplaces, gas furnaces and water heaters, and car engines. During power outages and winter storms, people bring these indoors or into garages, and CO poisonings spike. CDC calls CO a silent killer because you cannot see, smell, or taste it. A generator running inside a home or garage can kill within minutes, even with doors or windows open.

steps.title: Recognize the symptoms
steps.body: CDC lists headache, dizziness, weakness, upset stomach, vomiting, chest pain, and confusion. Higher levels cause seizures, loss of consciousness, and death. Symptoms are often mistaken for flu, but there is no fever, and several people - and pets - in the same building often feel sick at once and get better when they leave. People who are asleep or intoxicated can die without ever waking. Babies, older adults, pregnant women, and people with heart or lung disease are at highest risk.

steps.title: Get everyone out now
steps.body: If anyone has symptoms or a CO alarm sounds, get everyone, including pets, out into fresh air immediately. Do not stop to search for the source or open windows room by room. Do not go back inside until emergency responders say it is safe. If you must rescue someone who is unresponsive inside, take a deep breath of fresh air, get them out fast, and do not stay in the space - rescuers are often poisoned too.

steps.title: Call 911 and give care
steps.body: Call 911 from outside. Tell the dispatcher you suspect carbon monoxide and how many people are affected. Keep victims outside in fresh air, warm, and lying down or sitting quietly. If someone is unresponsive and not breathing normally, start CPR. If they are breathing but drowsy, place them in the recovery position. Anyone with symptoms should be checked at a hospital; emergency oxygen treatment clears CO from the blood faster, and some patients need specialized treatment.

steps.title: Use generators only outdoors and far away
steps.body: Never run a generator inside a home, garage, carport, basement, crawl space, or shed, even with doors open. CDC advises running it outdoors at least 20 feet (6 m) from doors, windows, and vents, with the exhaust pointed away from the building. Never use gas or charcoal grills, camp stoves, or fire pits indoors. Never heat a home with a gas oven or stove. Do not run a vehicle in an attached garage, and clear snow from the tailpipe before running a car parked outside.

steps.title: Install and maintain CO alarms
steps.body: Put battery-powered or battery-backup CO alarms outside each sleeping area and on every level of the home. Test them monthly and replace batteries as needed. Replace alarms about every 5 years or as the manufacturer directs, because sensors weaken. A CO alarm is different from a smoke alarm unless it is labeled as a combination unit. Keep a spare battery CO alarm for camping, cabins, and RVs.

steps.title: Find and fix the source
steps.body: After a CO event, have the fire department or a qualified technician check fuel-burning appliances, chimneys, and vents before anyone returns. Keep chimneys and flues clean and clear of nests and snow. If a gas appliance smells of gas, leave and call emergency services. Never patch over a problem by opening a window and continuing to use the appliance.

warnings: Never run a generator, grill, or camp stove indoors or in a garage - open doors do not make it safe.
Several people sick at once with headaches and nausea in the same building suggests CO - get out.
Do not re-enter a building with a sounding CO alarm until responders clear it.
Rescuers can be overcome too - get victims out fast and do not linger.
proTips: Buy a battery-powered CO alarm for your emergency kit before you buy the generator.
Mark a spot 20+ feet from the house for the generator and run a heavy-duty outdoor cord.
Pets that suddenly act sick or sleepy may be the first warning.
Write 'CO - test monthly' on alarms with the install date.

title: Snakebite - North America
summary: For a North American snakebite: get away from the snake, call 911, keep the person still with jewelry removed, mark the swelling, and get to a hospital for antivenom. No cutting, sucking, tourniquets, ice, or shocks.

steps.title: Get away from the snake
steps.body: Move the person and yourself out of striking range - a snake can strike about half its body length, and dead or decapitated snakes can still bite by reflex. Do not try to catch, kill, or carry the snake. If it is safe, take a photo from a distance to help identify it, but never delay care for this. Most U.S. venomous bites are from pit vipers (rattlesnakes, copperheads, cottonmouths); coral snakes are less common.

steps.title: Call 911 now
steps.body: The 2024 AHA/Red Cross first aid guidelines say to activate EMS for any bite from a venomous or possibly venomous snake. Do not wait for symptoms - some serious bites look minor at first, and coral snake symptoms can be delayed for hours. CDC/NIOSH advises not driving yourself to the hospital. Antivenom given in a hospital is the only effective treatment; your field job is to get the person there quickly and safely.

steps.title: Keep them still and calm
steps.body: Have the person sit or lie down and rest. AHA guidance supports resting and immobilizing the bitten limb and limiting exertion, as long as this does not delay getting to care. Keep the limb in a comfortable, neutral position at about heart level. If you must walk out, walk slowly and rest often. A loose splint can help keep the limb still.

steps.title: Remove rings and tight items
steps.body: Take off rings, watches, bracelets, anklets, and tight clothing or boots on the bitten limb right away, before swelling starts. Swelling from pit viper bites can be dramatic and fast, and a ring can cut off circulation to a finger. Gently wash the bite with soap and water if available, and cover it with a clean, dry, loose dressing.

steps.title: Mark the swelling and watch closely
steps.body: With a pen, mark the edge of swelling or tenderness and write the time next to it. Repeat every 15-30 minutes so hospital staff can see how fast it spreads. Watch for nausea or vomiting, a metallic or rubbery taste, numbness or tingling of the face or limbs, muscle twitching, weakness, trouble breathing or swallowing, drooping eyelids, bleeding from gums, or faintness. Write down the time of the bite.

steps.title: Know what NOT to do
steps.body: Current guidelines say these are harmful or useless: tourniquets or tight bands; cutting the wound; sucking out venom by mouth or with suction devices; ice or cold water; electric shock; and pressure-immobilization wraps, which are used for some snakes in other countries but are not recommended in North America. Do not give alcohol or caffeine. Do not give aspirin, ibuprofen, or naproxen because they can increase bleeding; Mayo Clinic notes acetaminophen is an option for pain.

steps.title: Get to definitive care
steps.body: Every suspected venomous bite needs hospital evaluation, even if it looks mild, because effects can worsen over hours. In a remote or grid-down setting, start moving toward the nearest hospital as soon as possible while keeping the person at rest; carrying them is better than letting them hike. Bring your swelling marks and timeline. Dry bites with no venom do happen, but only a medical team can safely decide that after observation.

warnings: Never cut, suck, ice, shock, or tourniquet a snakebite.
Do not handle the snake, even if it appears dead.
Do not give aspirin, ibuprofen, or naproxen after a snakebite.
Do not wait for symptoms before seeking care - delay worsens outcomes.
proTips: Wear boots and long pants, use a light at night, and never reach into spots you cannot see.
Keep a marker in your first aid kit for tracking swelling.
Know which hospitals in your area stock antivenom before you head out.
Commercial venom extractor kits do not work - leave them out of your kit.

title: Spider Bites and Scorpion Stings
summary: Clean and cool most spider bites and scorpion stings, recognize black widow, brown recluse, and bark scorpion warning signs, and know when to call Poison Help or 911.

steps.title: Most bites are minor
steps.body: Most spider bites cause only local pain, redness, and itching that heal in days. Many skin sores blamed on spiders are actually infections. The two spiders of medical concern in the U.S. are the black widow (shiny black with a red hourglass on the belly, found across much of the country, especially the South) and the brown recluse (brown with a violin-shaped mark on the back, mainly in the south-central and southern U.S.). The Arizona bark scorpion, found in the Southwest, is the U.S. scorpion that can cause serious illness.

steps.title: Basic first aid
steps.body: Move away from the spider or scorpion. Wash the bite with mild soap and water. Apply a cool cloth or ice wrapped in cloth for about 15 minutes at a time, each hour, to ease pain and swelling. Raise the limb if you can. Use an over-the-counter pain reliever as the label directs; AHA/Red Cross guidance supports acetaminophen or NSAIDs, topical lidocaine on intact skin, and ice for scorpion sting pain. For itching from a spider bite, an oral antihistamine or hydrocortisone cream may help. Keep the area clean to prevent infection.

steps.title: Black widow warning signs
steps.body: Black widow venom affects nerves. The bite may feel like a pinprick, followed within an hour or so by spreading pain, muscle cramps, and rigidity in the belly, back, chest, or limbs. Sweating, nausea, vomiting, headache, shaking, and anxiety may follow. Severe belly cramping can be mistaken for appendicitis. Anyone with these symptoms, especially children and older adults, needs medical care.

steps.title: Brown recluse warning signs
steps.body: Brown recluse bites are often painless at first. Over hours, the area may become painful, with a blister or sore that develops a dark blue or purple center surrounded by a pale or red ring. Some people develop fever, chills, and body aches. Rarely, the venom affects blood and kidneys - dark urine, yellow skin, or severe weakness need emergency care. Wounds can grow and heal slowly over weeks, so follow up with a clinician.

steps.title: Bark scorpion stings
steps.body: Most scorpion stings cause burning pain like a bee sting, sometimes with numbness and tingling that spreads. Severe stings - most likely in young children and older adults - can cause trouble coordinating muscles, roving or jerking eye movements, drooling, trouble breathing, fast heart rate, nausea, and fever. Call Poison Help at 1-800-222-1222 for any scorpion sting for advice. University of Arizona experts warn not to treat these nerve symptoms as an allergy; antihistamines and epinephrine are not the treatment.

steps.title: When to call 911 or get care
steps.body: AHA/Red Cross 2024 guidelines say to call EMS for body-wide symptoms such as trouble breathing, muscle rigidity, dizziness, or confusion. Seek medical care if pain spreads beyond the bite, becomes severe or is not controlled by OTC medicine, an open wound develops, or the skin around the bite becomes red, purple, or streaked with spreading swelling. Get care too if you are unsure what bit you and symptoms are worsening. Tetanus shots should be up to date.

steps.title: Prevent bites
steps.body: Shake out shoes, clothing, gloves, and bedding before use, especially in sheds, garages, and camps. Wear gloves when moving wood, rocks, or stored boxes. Move beds away from walls and keep bedding off the floor. In scorpion areas, a UV flashlight makes scorpions glow at night. Seal cracks and reduce clutter where spiders and scorpions hide.

warnings: Do not cut, suck, or apply a tourniquet to a spider bite or scorpion sting.
Children and older adults are most at risk from black widow and bark scorpion venom - get care early.
Trouble breathing, muscle rigidity, or confusion after a bite or sting is an emergency.
A spreading red, hot, painful area with fever is more likely infection - see medical-058.
proTips: If safe, take a photo of the spider or scorpion for identification - do not risk another bite.
Keep Poison Help 1-800-222-1222 saved; they handle bites and stings, not just poisons.
Store shoes upside down or in sealed bins in scorpion country.
Mark the edge of redness with a pen and note the time to track spread.

title: Bee, Wasp, and Fire Ant Stings
summary: Remove stingers fast, ease local pain and itching, handle fire ant pustules without infection, and recognize the signs of anaphylaxis that need epinephrine and 911.

steps.title: Get away first
steps.body: When bees or wasps are swarming, walk or run away quickly to a building, vehicle, or dense cover - do not swat, which can provoke more stings. Do not jump into water; insects may wait for you to surface. For fire ants, move off the mound immediately and brush ants off briskly with a hand or cloth, since they cling and sting repeatedly. Remove clothing they have crawled into.

steps.title: Remove a stinger quickly
steps.body: Honeybees leave a barbed stinger with a venom sac attached. The 2024 AHA/Red Cross first aid guidelines say removing a stinger left in the skin quickly is reasonable - by scraping with a fingernail or card edge or by pulling it out. Speed matters more than method, because the sac keeps pumping venom for a short time. Wasps, hornets, and yellow jackets usually do not leave stingers and can sting more than once.

steps.title: Treat local pain and itching
steps.body: Wash the area with soap and water. Apply a cold pack or ice wrapped in cloth to reduce pain and swelling. The AHA guidelines note that over-the-counter acetaminophen or NSAIDs may help pain, and oral antihistamines or hydrocortisone cream may relieve itching - follow each label. Large local swelling that spreads several inches over a day or two is common and is not, by itself, anaphylaxis, but have it checked if it is severe.

steps.title: Handle fire ant pustules
steps.body: Fire ant stings burn sharply, then form raised white pustules within about 24 hours. Mississippi State University Extension notes these pustules are not infected even though they look like it. Do not pop or scratch them; breaking them open invites infection, especially in people with diabetes or weak immune systems. Keep the area clean and covered if needed, and use cold packs and anti-itch products as labeled. Pustules can last several days to a week.

steps.title: Watch for anaphylaxis
steps.body: A small number of people have severe allergic reactions to stings, sometimes from a single sting. Danger signs anywhere on the body include hives spreading beyond the sting, swelling of the lips, tongue, or throat, hoarseness, trouble breathing or wheezing, vomiting, dizziness, fainting, or confusion. These usually begin within minutes. Treat this as anaphylaxis: use the person's epinephrine auto-injector as the device directs and call 911 - see guide medical-042.

steps.title: Know other reasons to get care
steps.body: Stings to the eye need evaluation by a medical professional, according to AHA guidance. Stings inside the mouth or throat can swell and block the airway - call 911. Many stings at once, as in a swarm attack or a fall onto a fire ant mound, can cause a toxic reaction even in people who are not allergic, especially children and older adults; seek medical care. Watch for infection signs over the next days: increasing redness, warmth, pus, red streaks, or fever.

steps.title: Prevent stings
steps.body: Wear shoes outdoors, keep sweet drinks covered, and check cans before sipping. Avoid strong perfumes and bright floral clothing near nests. Watch for fire ant mounds in sunny, grassy areas before sitting, kneeling, or setting gear down. People with a known sting allergy should carry two epinephrine devices at all times and wear medical ID.

warnings: Throat swelling, trouble breathing, or fainting after a sting is anaphylaxis - give epinephrine and call 911.
Antihistamines do not stop anaphylaxis - never use them instead of epinephrine.
Stings in the mouth, throat, or eye need urgent medical care.
Do not pop fire ant pustules - it raises infection risk.
proTips: Keep a plastic card in your kit for scraping out stingers.
Mark the edge of a large local reaction to see whether it is spreading.
Teach kids to walk away from buzzing insects instead of swatting.
If you have had a severe sting reaction before, ask an allergist about venom immunotherapy.
