Hives spreading, throat swelling, or trouble breathing: epinephrine and 911

title: Ticks - Removal and Tick-Borne Illness Signs
summary: Remove attached ticks quickly and correctly with tweezers, avoid myths that make things worse, and watch for the fever and rash that signal tick-borne illness.

steps.title: Find ticks early
steps.body: Ticks wait on grass and brush and crawl to warm, hidden spots. After time outdoors, check the whole body: scalp and hairline, in and behind the ears, neck, armpits, inside the belly button, around the waist, between the legs, and behind the knees. Check children, pets, and gear too. Many ticks are as small as a poppy seed. A shower soon after coming inside helps you find crawling ticks. The sooner a tick is removed, the lower the chance it passes on infection.

steps.title: Remove it right away with tweezers
steps.body: CDC and the 2024 AHA/Red Cross first aid guidelines agree: remove the tick as soon as possible. Use clean, fine-tipped tweezers or a tick-removal tool. Grasp the tick as close to the skin surface as you can, by its head or mouthparts, not its swollen body. Pull upward with steady, even pressure. Do not twist or jerk, which can break off the mouthparts. If you have no tweezers, use regular tweezers or fingers protected with tissue; do not wait for a clinic to do it.

steps.title: Skip the myths
steps.body: Do not paint the tick with nail polish or petroleum jelly, burn it with a match, or cover it with alcohol to make it 'back out.' CDC warns these methods can irritate the tick and may push infected fluid into the skin, and they waste time. If small mouthparts stay in the skin, remove them with tweezers only if it is easy; otherwise leave them and let the skin heal. They do not keep transmitting disease.

steps.title: Clean up and dispose
steps.body: Wash the bite area and your hands with soap and water, rubbing alcohol, or hand sanitizer. Kill a live tick by putting it in alcohol, sealing it in a bag or container, wrapping it tightly in tape, or flushing it. Never crush it with your fingers. Write down the date, where on the body it was attached, and where you likely picked it up. Testing the tick is generally not recommended because results do not tell you whether you are infected.

steps.title: Know when to call a clinician soon
steps.body: The AHA guidelines advise contacting a health care professional within 72 hours after removing an engorged (swollen, fed) tick in an area where Lyme disease is common. In some cases a clinician may recommend preventive treatment. Pregnant people, young children, and those with weak immune systems should also check in after any attached tick.

steps.title: Watch for illness for 30 days
steps.body: Tick-borne illnesses usually start days to weeks after the bite. Watch for fever, chills, headache, fatigue, muscle or joint aches, and any rash. Lyme disease often causes an expanding red rash, sometimes with a clear center like a bull's-eye, at or near the bite. Rocky Mountain spotted fever can cause small spots on the wrists, ankles, palms, or soles and can become deadly quickly - fever with headache after a tick bite needs prompt care. If you get sick, see a clinician and tell them about the bite, when it happened, and where.

steps.title: Prevent the next bite
steps.body: Use an EPA-registered repellent on skin as the label directs, and wear clothing treated with permethrin. Wear light-colored long pants tucked into socks. Walk in the center of trails. Dry clothes on high heat for 10 minutes or more after outings to kill ticks. Check pets daily and talk to a veterinarian about tick prevention.

warnings: Do not use heat, nail polish, petroleum jelly, or alcohol to remove a tick.
Do not squeeze or crush the tick's body.
Fever with headache or rash after a tick bite needs prompt medical care - some tick-borne illnesses become severe fast.
Do not rely on tick testing to rule out infection.
proTips: Keep fine-tipped tweezers in every kit - they make clean removal much easier.
Take a dated photo of the bite site each day for a week to spot an expanding rash.
Use a lint roller on clothes after hikes to catch crawling ticks.
Set a phone reminder for 30 days after the bite to review any symptoms.
source: CDC / AHA-American Red Cross First Aid 2024

sources.title: Removing a Tick
2024 American Heart Association and American Red Cross Guidelines for First Aid - Tick Bites
sources.publisher: American Heart Association / American Red Cross

whenNotTo: Do not delay removal to wait for a clinic.
Do not dig deeply into skin to chase small leftover mouthparts.

quickGlance.situation: You find a tick attached to skin.
immediate: Grasp it close to the skin with fine-tipped tweezers
Pull straight up with steady, even pressure - no twisting
Clean the bite and your hands; seal or drown the tick
then: Call a clinician within 72 hours for an engorged tick in a Lyme area
Watch 30 days for fever, rash, or aches and report the bite

title: Animal Bites and Rabies Exposure
summary: Wash every animal bite or scratch with soap and water for 15 minutes, control bleeding, and get medical care quickly to decide on rabies shots - rabies is almost always fatal once symptoms start, but prevention works.

steps.title: Get safe and stop bleeding
steps.body: Move away from the animal and do not try to catch it yourself. If the wound is bleeding heavily, press firmly with a clean cloth until it stops; for life-threatening limb bleeding, use the steps in medical-002. Most bites bleed modestly. If you can do so safely, note what the animal looked like, where it went, and whether it is a pet with an owner you can identify.

steps.title: Wash the wound for 15 minutes
steps.body: Public health agencies advise washing every bite and scratch right away with soap and running water for a full 15 minutes. This is one of the most effective things you can do to lower the risk of rabies and infection. If available, apply an antiseptic such as povidone-iodine afterward. Rinse deep punctures thoroughly. Then cover with a clean dressing. Also wash any spot where an animal's saliva touched broken skin, eyes, nose, or mouth.

steps.title: Get medical care promptly
steps.body: See a doctor, urgent care, or emergency department the same day for any bite that breaks the skin, any wild animal bite or scratch, and any bat contact. Tell them what animal it was and where it happened. Bites to the face, hands, feet, or joints, deep punctures, and bites in people with diabetes or weak immune systems have high infection risk. The clinician will check whether a tetanus shot is needed and whether rabies shots are needed.

steps.title: Know the high-risk animals
steps.body: In the U.S., bats, raccoons, skunks, and foxes are the main rabies carriers, and coyotes and other wild carnivores are also high risk. Bats are especially dangerous because their bites can be too small to see or feel. If a bat is found in a room where someone was sleeping, or near a child or anyone who cannot reliably say what happened, treat it as a possible exposure even with no visible bite. Never handle a bat with bare hands. Small rodents (mice, rats, squirrels) and rabbits rarely carry rabies.

steps.title: Dogs, cats, and observation
steps.body: A dog or cat that bites someone is usually observed for at least 10 days. If the animal stays healthy during that time, it could not have passed on rabies at the time of the bite. Get the owner's name, phone number, and vaccine records. Stray, unknown, or sick-acting animals raise the risk. Report bites to the local health department or animal control as local law requires.

steps.title: Do not wait for symptoms
steps.body: Rabies post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) is a series of vaccine shots and, for people not previously vaccinated, an immune globulin injection. It is nearly 100% effective when started before symptoms appear. Once symptoms begin - fever, tingling at the bite, agitation, confusion, trouble swallowing - there is no cure. Start the evaluation right away; delays shrink the safety margin.

steps.title: Watch for infection
steps.body: Over the next few days, check for increasing redness, swelling, warmth, pus, red streaks, fever, or worsening pain. Cat bites in particular often become infected quickly. Infection after a bite needs medical care and often antibiotics prescribed by a clinician. In a grid-down situation, keep the wound clean, change dressings daily, and evacuate for care if infection signs appear - see medical-058.

warnings: Any bat contact, or a bat found in a room with a sleeping person or child, needs medical evaluation for rabies.
Do not wait for rabies symptoms - by then it is too late for treatment.
Do not try to capture a wild or strange animal yourself.
Bites to the hand, face, or joints and cat bites are high infection risk - get care the same day.
proTips: Keep pets' rabies vaccinations current - it protects your family too.
If a bat must be captured for testing, use thick gloves and a container, never bare hands.
Photograph the wound and the animal (from a distance) for the clinician.
Write down the date, time, place, and animal details for the health department.
source: Los Angeles County Department of Public Health (Veterinary Public Health)

sources.title: About Rabies - What to Do After an Animal Bite
sources.publisher: Los Angeles County Department of Public Health

whenNotTo: Do not close deep bite wounds tightly with tape or glue in the field - they trap bacteria; leave closure to a clinician.
Do not skip care because the animal 'looked healthy'.

quickGlance.situation: A person is bitten or scratched by an animal, or had contact with a bat.
immediate: Get away from the animal; press to stop bleeding
Wash the wound with soap and running water for 15 minutes
Get medical care the same day to assess rabies and tetanus
then: Record the animal, owner, and location; report as local law requires
Watch for redness, pus, red streaks, or fever

title: Mild and Moderate Allergic Reactions
summary: Manage hives, itching, sneezing, and contact rashes like poison ivy with trigger removal and over-the-counter products, while watching closely for signs that a reaction is turning into anaphylaxis.

steps.title: Sort mild from severe
steps.body: Mild to moderate reactions stay in one body area or are limited to the skin and nose: a few hives, itchy skin, watery itchy eyes, sneezing, a runny nose, or an itchy contact rash. Anaphylaxis is different - it involves breathing, throat swelling, circulation, or several body systems at once, such as hives plus vomiting, or hives plus dizziness. If you see any trouble breathing, throat or tongue swelling, hoarseness, repeated vomiting, faintness, or confusion, stop here and go to medical-042: give epinephrine and call 911.

steps.title: Remove the trigger
steps.body: Stop eating the suspect food, move away from the plant, animal, or insect, and take off contaminated clothing or jewelry. If the reaction started after a new medicine, do not take another dose and contact the prescriber or pharmacist. Write down what the person ate, touched, or took in the past few hours. Knowing the trigger helps prevent the next, possibly worse, reaction.

steps.title: Wash off plant oils fast
steps.body: For poison ivy, oak, or sumac, the 2024 AHA/Red Cross first aid guidelines recommend washing exposed skin with soap and water or a commercial decontamination product as soon as possible, ideally within minutes. Wash under fingernails and clean clothing, tools, and pet fur that touched the plant, because the oil spreads. The rash itself is not contagious once the oil is washed away.

steps.title: Use OTC relief as labeled
steps.body: An oral antihistamine can ease hives, itching, sneezing, and watery eyes - follow the label for age and dose. Some older antihistamines cause strong drowsiness and should not be taken before driving or by people who must stay alert on watch. Hydrocortisone cream may help small itchy patches. For plant rashes, AHA guidance says cool compresses and oatmeal baths may be considered; OTC steroid creams and antihistamines have uncertain benefit but are low risk when used as labeled.

steps.title: Comfort the skin
steps.body: Apply cool, wet cloths for 15-20 minutes several times a day. Keep fingernails short and discourage scratching, which can break the skin and cause infection. Wear loose cotton clothing. Calamine lotion can soothe itching. Avoid hot showers, which often worsen itching.

steps.title: Watch for the reaction to grow
steps.body: Stay with the person for at least an hour after a new reaction and check every few minutes at first. Reactions to foods, stings, and medicines can escalate. If hives spread rapidly over the body, or any breathing, throat, stomach, or circulation symptoms appear, treat as anaphylaxis immediately. People with asthma and a food allergy are at higher risk of severe reactions.

steps.title: Know when to see a clinician
steps.body: Get medical care for a rash on the face, eyes, or genitals; a rash covering large areas; blisters that ooze or show signs of infection; swelling of the eyelids that closes the eye; or hives that keep coming back for days. Anyone who has had a reaction to a food, sting, or medicine should ask about seeing an allergist and whether they need to carry epinephrine.

warnings: Trouble breathing, throat swelling, or faintness means anaphylaxis - use epinephrine and call 911, not antihistamines.
Some antihistamines cause heavy drowsiness - do not drive or stand watch after taking them.
Do not burn poison ivy - the smoke can cause severe lung reactions.
Do not give a medicine again after it caused a reaction.
proTips: Keep a non-drowsy antihistamine and hydrocortisone cream in every kit.
Learn to spot 'leaves of three' poison ivy and oak in your area.
Keep a written allergy list for each family member in your go-bag.
Wash with soap and plenty of water - the oil comes off best in the first minutes.
source: AHA-American Red Cross First Aid 2024 / FDA

sources.title: 2024 American Heart Association and American Red Cross Guidelines for First Aid
sources.publisher: American Heart Association / American Red Cross

sources.title: FDA Approves First Nasal Spray for Treatment of Anaphylaxis (signs of anaphylaxis)

whenNotTo: Do not treat a reaction with only antihistamines when there are breathing, throat, or circulation symptoms.
Do not use this guide for a person with a known severe allergy who has been exposed to their trigger - follow their anaphylaxis plan.

quickGlance.situation: Someone has hives, itching, sneezing, or a contact rash with no breathing or throat trouble.
immediate: Remove the trigger; wash plant oils off with soap and water right away
Give an OTC antihistamine per the label; cool compresses for itch
Watch closely for spreading hives or breathing trouble
then: Any throat, breathing, or faintness symptoms: epinephrine and 911
See a clinician for face or eye rashes, large areas, or infection

title: Fainting - Prevent, Respond, and Red Flags
summary: Stop a faint before it happens with sitting or lying down and leg counterpressure maneuvers, care for someone who has fainted, and recognize the warning signs that fainting is a heart or brain emergency.

steps.title: Recognize a coming faint
steps.body: Many faints are preceded by warning signs called presyncope: lightheadedness, feeling hot or sweaty, nausea, pale skin, yawning, tunnel or blurred vision, ringing ears, and weakness. Common triggers are standing a long time, standing up quickly, heat, dehydration, pain, the sight of blood, fear, and skipping meals. These 'vasovagal' and posture-related faints are usually harmless in themselves, but the fall can cause serious injury.

steps.title: Get them down safely
steps.body: The 2024 AHA/Red Cross first aid guidelines say a person with these warning signs should sit or lie down in a safe position right away. Lying flat is best. Guide them down so they do not fall, away from stairs, edges, traffic, and hard objects. If they can lie down, raising the legs a little can help. Loosen tight collars and belts, and move them into shade or cooler air if heat is a factor.

steps.title: Use counterpressure maneuvers
steps.body: Once the person is in a safe position, physical counterpressure maneuvers can help prevent the faint. The guidelines say lower-body maneuvers may work better than upper-body ones. Examples: cross the legs and squeeze the thighs and buttocks together hard, or squat; while lying down, tense the leg muscles. Hold for 30 seconds or more and repeat. Do not use these maneuvers if the warning signs come with signs of a heart attack or stroke - chest pain, face droop, arm weakness, or slurred speech.

steps.title: If they faint
steps.body: A person who has fainted usually wakes within a minute once they are lying flat. Check that they are breathing normally. If they are breathing but not yet awake, roll them onto their side in the recovery position, unless you suspect a neck or back injury from the fall. If they are not breathing normally, call 911 and start CPR. Look for injuries from the fall, especially to the head and face.

steps.title: Know when to call 911
steps.body: Per the AHA guidelines, activate EMS if symptoms do not improve within 1-2 minutes, if the person actually faints, or if symptoms worsen or come back. Call immediately for fainting with chest pain, a racing or irregular heartbeat, shortness of breath, a severe headache, confusion, weakness on one side, seizure activity, fainting during exercise or while lying down, fainting with no warning, an injury from the fall, pregnancy, or in someone with known heart disease.

steps.title: Help them recover slowly
steps.body: Keep the person lying down for 10-15 minutes after they feel better. Then have them sit for a few minutes before standing, with someone beside them. Once fully alert and able to swallow, give water, and food if they skipped a meal. Do not let them drive or stand watch until they have fully recovered and the cause is understood.

steps.title: Prevent repeat episodes
steps.body: Drink enough fluids, especially in heat. Stand up slowly in stages. Avoid long periods of standing still; shift weight and flex calf muscles. People who know their triggers, such as needles or blood, should lie down beforehand. Anyone who faints for the first time, faints repeatedly, or has any of the red flags above should be evaluated by a clinician, because heart rhythm problems can cause faints.

warnings: Fainting during exercise, while lying down, or with chest pain or palpitations can signal a dangerous heart problem - call 911.
Do not prop a fainting person upright or hold them standing - get them flat.
Do not splash water, give smelling salts, or slap the face.
Do not give food or drink until they are fully awake and can swallow.
proTips: Teach the 'cross and squeeze' leg maneuver to anyone who faints at blood draws.
In heat, drink regularly and rest in shade before people get lightheaded.
Check blood sugar in people with diabetes who feel faint - see medical-045.
Note what the person was doing and how long they were out for the clinician.
source: AHA-American Red Cross First Aid 2024

sources.title: 2024 American Heart Association and American Red Cross Guidelines for First Aid - Presyncope
sources.publisher: American Heart Association / American Red Cross

whenNotTo: Do not use counterpressure maneuvers when faintness comes with signs of heart attack or stroke.
Do not move a person who fell and may have a neck or back injury unless the area is unsafe.

quickGlance.situation: Someone feels lightheaded, pale, and sweaty as if about to faint - or has fainted.
immediate: Get them sitting or lying down in a safe spot right away
Have them cross legs and squeeze thighs hard, or squat
If they faint: check breathing, recovery position, CPR if not breathing normally
then: Call 911 if no improvement in 1-2 minutes, they faint, or red flags appear
Keep them lying 10-15 minutes; stand up slowly with help

title: Abdominal Emergencies - Red Flags
summary: Tell ordinary stomach upset from belly pain that needs a surgeon - appendicitis, bowel obstruction, ectopic pregnancy, and other red flags - and know what to do while you arrange evacuation.

steps.title: Know when belly pain is an emergency
steps.body: Most stomach aches from gas, mild food illness, or constipation pass within hours. The American College of Emergency Physicians advises emergency care when pain is sudden and severe, does not ease within about 30 minutes, or comes with continuous vomiting. Other red flags: a hard, rigid, or very tender belly; pain that makes the person lie very still or curl up; fever with belly pain; vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds; black, tarry, or bloody stool; fainting; and pain in pregnancy.

steps.title: Suspect appendicitis
steps.body: Appendicitis often starts as a vague ache around the belly button that moves over hours to the lower right abdomen and becomes sharp. It usually comes with loss of appetite, nausea or vomiting, and low fever. Pain worsens with walking, coughing, or bumps in the road. It needs urgent surgery; delay can let the appendix burst and cause a life-threatening infection. In children and pregnant women, the pain may be in unusual places.

steps.title: Suspect bowel obstruction
steps.body: A blocked intestine causes cramping pain that comes in waves, a swollen or bloated belly, vomiting (sometimes green or foul-smelling), and inability to pass gas or stool. It is more likely in people who have had abdominal surgery, hernias, or certain cancers. A tender bulge at a hernia site that cannot be pushed back is also an emergency. Do not give laxatives or enemas for suspected obstruction.

steps.title: Think about ectopic pregnancy
steps.body: In anyone who could be pregnant, severe lower belly or pelvic pain - especially on one side - with vaginal bleeding or spotting, dizziness, fainting, or shoulder-tip pain may be an ectopic pregnancy bleeding inside the abdomen. This can be fatal quickly. Ask about a missed or late period. Treat it as an emergency even if the person does not know they are pregnant.

steps.title: Other dangerous causes
steps.body: Sudden severe upper or middle belly pain with vomiting, fever, and a fast pulse may be pancreatitis. Sudden severe pain can also come from a perforated ulcer or, in older adults, a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm - often with back pain and fainting. Upper belly pain with sweating and shortness of breath can be a heart attack (see medical-040). Severe right upper pain with fever and yellow skin can be a gallbladder problem.

steps.title: What to do while getting help
steps.body: Call 911 or arrange the fastest evacuation for any red flag. Let the person lie in the position of greatest comfort, often on their side with knees bent. Give nothing to eat or drink in case they need surgery; small sips or wetting the lips is acceptable if transport will be very long and they are not vomiting. Do not give laxatives, enemas, or strong pain relievers that might hide worsening signs, and avoid heating pads on a possible appendicitis. Watch for shock: pale, cold, clammy skin, fast pulse, and confusion (see medical-006).

steps.title: Monitor and record
steps.body: Write down when the pain started, where it began and where it moved, what makes it worse, vomiting and stool details, temperature, pulse, and the date of the last menstrual period if relevant. Recheck every 30 minutes. Pain that steadily gets worse, spreads across the whole belly, or comes with a rising pulse means deterioration. In a grid-down setting, these conditions cannot be treated in the field; evacuation to surgical care is the treatment.

warnings: Severe belly pain with vaginal bleeding or fainting in someone who could be pregnant is an emergency.
A rigid, board-like belly or pain with shock signs needs immediate evacuation.
Do not give laxatives or enemas for severe belly pain, especially with vomiting and bloating.
Vomiting blood or passing black or bloody stool needs emergency care.
proTips: Ask the person to hop or cough - sharply increased pain suggests irritation of the belly lining.
Track the pain location on a simple drawing to show the clinician.
Keep a pregnancy test in your medical kit; it changes decisions fast.
Older adults and people with diabetes may have serious problems with milder pain - lower your threshold to seek care.
source: American College of Emergency Physicians

sources.title: Know When to Go - Stomach Pain

whenNotTo: Do not 'wait and see' overnight with red-flag pain - surgical problems worsen with time.
Do not use this guide to rule out a problem; only a clinician with exam and tests can do that.

quickGlance.situation: Someone has severe, worsening, or unusual belly pain.
immediate: Call 911 for sudden severe pain, pain over 30 minutes, constant vomiting, or a rigid belly
Think ectopic pregnancy for pelvic pain with bleeding or fainting
Let them lie comfortably; nothing to eat or drink
then: No laxatives, enemas, or heat; watch for shock
Record pain location, timing, vomiting, and vital signs every 30 minutes

title: Emergency Childbirth When Help Can't Arrive
summary: Support a normal birth when no midwife or EMS can get there in time: prepare, let the baby come, keep the newborn warm and breathing, wait on the cord and placenta, and control bleeding afterward.

steps.title: Call for help and judge timing
steps.body: Call 911 if there is any service - dispatchers can coach you step by step. Signs birth is close: contractions less than 2 minutes apart, a strong urge to push, the baby's head showing (crowning), or the mother saying the baby is coming. If birth is not close and safe transport exists, go. If it is imminent, stay and prepare. Most births go normally; your job is mainly to support, keep things clean, and keep mother and baby warm.

steps.title: Prepare the space
steps.body: Wash your hands well and wear gloves if you have them. Lay down clean sheets, towels, or plastic covered with cloth. Gather several clean towels or blankets for the baby, a hat or cloth for the baby's head, clean string or shoelaces and new or boiled scissors or a blade for the cord if needed, a bowl or bag for the placenta, and pads or cloths for bleeding. Let the mother choose a comfortable position, such as semi-sitting with knees bent or on hands and knees.

steps.title: Support the baby's birth
steps.body: Let the mother push with contractions. As the head appears, support it gently with a light, flat hand - never pull on the baby's head or body. Gentle pressure on the skin below the vaginal opening may reduce tearing. Once the head is out, feel at the neck for the cord; if it is looped around, gently slip it over the head or loosen it. The shoulders usually follow with the next push; guide the baby out and hold firmly - newborns are slippery.

steps.title: Dry, stimulate, and warm the baby
steps.body: Immediately dry the baby with a towel and rub the back and head to stimulate breathing, then remove the wet towel. If the baby is pink or getting pinker, breathing, and crying or moving, place them skin-to-skin on the mother's chest or belly and cover both with a dry blanket, including the baby's head. If the baby is limp, pale or blue, or not breathing after about 30 seconds of drying and rubbing, start breaths for the baby within the first minute of life - do not wait for help. Lay the baby on their back on a firm surface, wipe mucus from the mouth and then the nose, tilt the head just slightly (sniffing position), and cover the baby's mouth and nose with your mouth. Give small, gentle puffs - just enough to see the chest rise - about one every 1 to 2 seconds (40 to 60 a minute). Keep going until the baby breathes or cries on their own or help takes over. If the baby still shows no signs of life after about 1 minute of breaths, start infant CPR (see CPR and AED - Adult, Child, and Infant). Breaths matter most for a newborn.

steps.title: Wait on the cord
steps.body: Do not pull on the cord. EMS protocols favor delayed cord clamping: leave the cord attached and pulsing for at least 1 minute, or until it stops pulsing, so the baby receives extra blood. If help is coming, you can leave the cord uncut. If you must cut it, tie it tightly with clean string in two places a few inches apart, starting several inches from the baby's belly, and cut between the ties with a clean blade.

steps.title: Let the placenta come on its own
steps.body: The placenta usually delivers within about 30 minutes, often with a small gush of blood and more cramping. Do not pull on the cord to hurry it. Catch it in a bowl or bag and keep it for the medical team to check that it is complete. Do not delay travel to a hospital just to wait for the placenta. Putting the baby to the breast helps the uterus contract.

steps.title: Control bleeding and watch for danger
steps.body: Some bleeding is normal. If bleeding continues after the placenta is out, firmly rub the lower belly below the belly button with a flat hand for about 15 seconds at a time until the uterus feels firm like a grapefruit. Heavy bleeding that soaks pads quickly, or dizziness, pale skin, and a fast pulse, is an emergency. Get trained help immediately for a breech birth (feet or buttocks first), a cord coming out before the baby, a baby stuck at the shoulders, or a very premature baby.

warnings: Never pull on the baby, the cord, or the placenta.
A cord that comes out before the baby, a breech birth, or a stuck shoulder needs trained help immediately.
Heavy bleeding after birth can kill quickly - massage the uterus and get emergency care.
Keep the newborn warm and dry; babies lose heat fast, especially through the head.
proTips: Pack a simple birth kit in your medical bag: gloves, towels, cord ties, a clean blade, pads, and a baby hat.
Write down the time of birth and when the placenta came out.
Skin-to-skin contact warms the baby and helps the mother's bleeding slow.
Stay calm and talk the mother through each step - your voice steadies the room.
source: San Francisco EMS Agency Protocol 5.03 (Childbirth)

sources.title: EMSA Protocol 5.03 - Childbirth: Normal Delivery and Post-Delivery Care
sources.publisher: San Francisco Emergency Medical Services Agency

whenNotTo: Do not attempt a home delivery when safe transport to a hospital or birth center is available and birth is not imminent.
Do not try to turn a breech baby or push a prolapsed cord back - get trained help.

quickGlance.situation: A baby is coming and no midwife, doctor, or EMS can arrive in time.
immediate: Call 911 for coaching if possible; wash hands and lay out clean towels
Support the head gently - never pull; slip a neck cord over the head
Dry, rub, and place the baby skin-to-skin; cover both
then: Wait at least 1 minute before clamping; let the placenta come on its own
Massage the lower belly for heavy bleeding and get emergency care

title: Altitude Illness - AMS, HAPE, and HACE
summary: Prevent altitude sickness with a slow ascent, recognize acute mountain sickness and its deadly forms (HAPE in the lungs, HACE in the brain), and know that descent is the most important treatment.

steps.title: Know who is at risk
steps.body: Altitude illness can start as low as about 6,500 ft (2,000 m) and becomes common above about 8,200 ft (2,500 m) in people who have not acclimatized. The altitude where you sleep matters more than where you hike during the day. Fitness does not protect you. People who have had HAPE or HACE before are at high risk of getting it again. Rapid ascent - driving or flying to a high trailhead and climbing the same day - is the biggest risk factor.

steps.title: Ascend slowly
steps.body: The Wilderness Medical Society guideline, as summarized by American Family Physician, recommends spending at least two days getting to a sleeping altitude of 8,200-9,800 ft (2,500-3,000 m). Above that, raise your sleeping altitude no more than about 1,600 ft (500 m) per night, and take a rest day at the same altitude after every 3,300 ft (1,000 m) gained. 'Climb high, sleep low' helps. Drink enough to keep urine light-colored, avoid alcohol and sleeping pills early on, and ask a clinician before the trip about preventive prescription medicine if you are at higher risk.

steps.title: Recognize acute mountain sickness (AMS)
steps.body: AMS feels like a hangover: headache plus one or more of nausea or vomiting, fatigue, dizziness, poor appetite, and trouble sleeping, usually starting 6-12 hours after arriving at a new altitude. Assume any illness at altitude is altitude illness until proven otherwise. For mild AMS, stop going up. Rest at the same altitude until symptoms resolve, usually in 1-3 days. Acetaminophen or ibuprofen used as labeled can ease the headache but do not treat the illness itself. If symptoms worsen despite rest, go down.

steps.title: Recognize HACE - swelling of the brain
steps.body: High-altitude cerebral edema (HACE) is AMS that has progressed to affect the brain. Key signs are loss of coordination (stumbling, unable to walk heel-to-toe in a straight line), confusion, unusual behavior, extreme drowsiness, and eventually coma. Test anyone with AMS by having them walk a straight line heel-to-toe. HACE can kill within hours. The person must descend immediately, with helpers - do not let them go down alone.

steps.title: Recognize HAPE - fluid in the lungs
steps.body: High-altitude pulmonary edema (HAPE) can occur with or without AMS, often on the second to fourth night at altitude. Early signs are reduced ability to exercise and breathlessness with exertion that is out of proportion to others in the group, plus a dry cough. Later signs are breathlessness at rest, a fast heart rate, bluish lips, crackling breath sounds, and cough with pink, frothy spit. HAPE is the most common cause of altitude-related death. Descend at once, minimizing exertion - carry the person if possible.

steps.title: Descend - the key treatment
steps.body: For severe AMS, HACE, or HAPE, descend. WMS guidance suggests going down 1,000-3,300 ft (300-1,000 m), or until symptoms clearly improve; for HAPE, at least 3,300 ft (1,000 m). Descend even at night if the person is getting worse and it can be done safely. Keep the person warm. If descent is truly impossible because of weather or terrain, supplemental oxygen or a portable hyperbaric (pressure) bag can buy time, and prescription medicines carried on clinician advice may help - but they are a bridge to descent, not a replacement.

steps.title: After recovery
steps.body: Someone with mild AMS can resume a slow ascent once all symptoms are gone. Anyone who had HACE or HAPE should not go back up on that trip without medical advice and should be evaluated by a clinician. Rule out other causes of symptoms - dehydration, low blood sugar, hypothermia, pneumonia, or carbon monoxide from cooking in a tent.

warnings: Never ascend with symptoms of altitude illness.
Stumbling, confusion, or breathlessness at rest at altitude is an emergency - descend now.
Never send a person with altitude illness down alone.
Medicines do not replace descent for HACE or HAPE.
proTips: Plan your sleeping altitudes on the map before the trip.
Watch each other - people with HACE often do not realize they are impaired.
Use the heel-to-toe walk test on anyone with a bad headache at altitude.
Never cook inside a closed tent - carbon monoxide symptoms mimic altitude sickness.
source: Wilderness Medical Society (via American Family Physician summary)

sources.title: Acute Altitude Illness: Updated Prevention and Treatment Guidelines from the Wilderness Medical Society

whenNotTo: Do not wait at altitude for medicine to work when someone has HACE or HAPE and descent is possible.
Do not use 'it's just a headache' to keep climbing - stop and reassess.

quickGlance.situation: Someone at high altitude has a headache, nausea, unusual breathlessness, or confusion.
immediate: Stop going up; assume altitude illness
Check walking heel-to-toe; stumbling or confusion means HACE - descend now
Breathless at rest or pink frothy cough means HAPE - descend now with minimal exertion
then: Descend 1,000-3,300 ft (at least 3,300 ft for HAPE) until better
Mild AMS: rest at the same altitude until symptoms are gone

title: Infection and Sepsis Recognition
summary: Spot a wound or body infection early, recognize the warning signs of sepsis - the body's life-threatening reaction to infection - and get emergency care fast, because sepsis is a time-critical emergency.

steps.title: Understand sepsis
steps.body: Sepsis happens when the body's response to an infection starts damaging its own organs. It can begin from any infection: an infected cut or bite, pneumonia, a urinary tract infection, a skin infection, or an abdominal infection. Without fast treatment it can lead to shock, organ failure, and death. Babies, older adults, people with diabetes, cancer, kidney or lung disease, weak immune systems, and people recovering from injury or surgery are at greatest risk.

steps.title: Watch wounds daily
steps.body: Look at every wound at least once a day. Mild redness and swelling right at the edges in the first day or two is normal healing. Warning signs of infection are redness that spreads outward, increasing swelling, warmth, worsening pain after the first couple of days, pus or cloudy drainage, a bad smell, red streaks running up the limb, and swollen tender lumps in the armpit or groin. Draw around the edge of redness with a pen and note the time to see if it spreads.

steps.title: Know the sepsis warning signs
steps.body: CDC lists these signs of sepsis: fever, chills, or feeling very cold; cold, clammy, or sweaty skin; sudden or worsening confusion or disorientation; trouble breathing or fast breathing; a fast heartbeat or low blood pressure (dizziness, fainting); and extreme pain or discomfort. People often describe feeling the sickest they have ever felt. Very little urine is another warning sign. Not everyone has a fever - some people, especially the elderly, have a low temperature instead.

steps.title: Act fast - call 911
steps.body: If someone with a known or suspected infection shows any sepsis signs, call 911 or get to an emergency department immediately and say 'I am worried about sepsis.' Every hour of delay raises the risk of death. Hospitals treat sepsis with IV antibiotics, fluids, and support for failing organs - care that cannot be replaced in the field. Bring a list of the person's medicines, allergies, and conditions, and tell the team where the infection started.

steps.title: Support the person while waiting
steps.body: Keep the person lying down and warm if they are cold or shivering; cool them gently if they are overheated. If they are alert and can swallow, offer sips of water or oral rehydration solution. If they are drowsy but breathing, place them on their side. Check and write down pulse, breathing rate, temperature, alertness, and urine every 15-30 minutes. If they stop breathing normally, start CPR.

steps.title: Prevent infections in the first place
steps.body: Clean every wound promptly with plenty of safe water and cover it with a clean dressing; change it when wet or dirty. Wash hands before and after wound care. Keep vaccines, including tetanus, up to date. Treat dehydration and keep people with chronic illness on their usual medicines. Do not ignore a urinary infection, cough with fever, or a skin infection that is spreading - early treatment prevents sepsis.

steps.title: Grid-down decisions
steps.body: When help is far away, decide early. A spreading infection, fever with any wound, or any sepsis sign means start evacuation now, not tomorrow. Antibiotics should be used only under a clinician's direction, by radio, phone, or telemedicine if possible; the wrong drug or dose wastes precious time. Keep a written log of signs and times so whoever receives the patient can act quickly.

warnings: Confusion, fast breathing, clammy skin, or feeling extremely ill with an infection can be sepsis - call 911.
Red streaks spreading from a wound are a sign of spreading infection - get care the same day.
Do not wait for a fever; older adults may have normal or low temperatures with sepsis.
Do not take or give prescription antibiotics without a clinician's direction.
proTips: Mark the edge of redness with a pen and the time - spreading lines tell the story clearly.
Say the word 'sepsis' to dispatchers and emergency staff to speed evaluation.
A cheap thermometer and pulse oximeter make your observations far more useful.
Infection signs after a bite, burn, or puncture wound deserve extra caution.
source: U.S. CDC

sources.title: Sepsis Signs and Symptoms (EMS card)

whenNotTo: Do not treat suspected sepsis at home when emergency care is reachable.
Do not squeeze or cut open an infected wound in the field - it can spread infection.

quickGlance.situation: Someone with an infection or wound becomes confused, breathes fast, has clammy skin, or feels extremely ill.
immediate: Call 911 or go to the ER now and say 'sepsis'
Keep them lying down, warm or cool as needed; sips if alert
Recovery position if drowsy; CPR if not breathing normally
then: Record pulse, breathing, temperature, alertness every 15-30 minutes
Check all wounds daily and mark spreading redness

title: Dental Emergencies - Knocked-Out Tooth, Abscess, Broken Tooth
summary: Save a knocked-out adult tooth by replanting it or keeping it moist and getting to a dentist within 30 minutes, protect a broken tooth, and recognize a dental abscess that can become dangerous.

steps.title: Find the tooth and handle it right
steps.body: If a permanent (adult) tooth is knocked out, find it right away. The American Association of Endodontists says to pick it up by the crown - the white chewing part - and never touch the root. If it is dirty, rinse it briefly with water only. Do not scrub it, use soap or chemicals, dry it, or wrap it in tissue or cloth. The living cells on the root die quickly when they dry out.

steps.title: Put it back if you can
steps.body: The best place for a knocked-out adult tooth is back in its socket, as soon as possible. Gently push it in facing the right way, then hold it in place with a finger or by gently biting on a clean cloth. Do not force it. Do not replant a baby tooth - it can damage the adult tooth growing underneath; just bring the child to a dentist. Do not try to replant if the person is not fully alert or could inhale the tooth.

steps.title: If not, keep it moist
steps.body: If you cannot replant it, keep the tooth moist. The AAE recommends milk, an emergency tooth-preservation kit such as Save-a-Tooth, or holding it in the mouth next to the cheek (only for an older child or adult who will not swallow it). Do not store it in plain tap water, which damages root cells over time; some public health handouts list cool water only as a last resort. Act within 30 minutes and get to a dentist or endodontist with the tooth. Teeth can sometimes be saved even after an hour or more.

steps.title: Broken or chipped tooth
steps.body: Rinse the mouth gently with warm water. Save any large pieces in milk or a clean container. Put a cold compress on the face over the injured area to reduce swelling. If there is bleeding, press gently with clean gauze. Cover a sharp edge with dental wax or sugar-free gum to protect the tongue and cheek. See a dentist as soon as possible; a break that shows pink or red in the center has exposed the nerve and needs prompt care.

steps.title: Toothache and abscess
steps.body: For a toothache, rinse with warm water and gently floss to remove trapped food. Use a cold compress on the cheek if there is swelling, and an OTC pain reliever as the label directs. Do not put aspirin or heat directly on the tooth or gum - it can burn tissue. An abscess is a pocket of infection that may cause throbbing pain, a bad taste, a pimple-like bump on the gum, swelling of the face or jaw, and fever. Warm salt-water rinses may soothe the gum, but an abscess will not heal on its own and needs a dentist.

steps.title: Know the dangerous signs
steps.body: Dental infections can spread to the face, neck, and blood. Go to an emergency department right away for swelling that spreads to the eye or neck, trouble swallowing or breathing, inability to open the mouth, high fever, or feeling very ill - these can be life-threatening. Also seek emergency care for a jaw that may be broken, bleeding that will not stop after 15 minutes of firm pressure, or any dental injury with a head injury.

steps.title: Lip, tongue, and stuck objects
steps.body: For a bitten lip or tongue, press with a clean cloth and apply a cold compress; go to the emergency room if bleeding does not stop. For something stuck between teeth, use dental floss gently. Never use a pin, knife, or other sharp object to dig it out. In a grid-down setting, prevention matters most: brush twice daily, floss, and pack a small dental kit with floss, wax, gauze, and a temporary filling material.

warnings: Never replant a baby tooth.
Do not touch the root of a knocked-out tooth or let it dry.
Facial swelling spreading toward the eye or neck, or trouble swallowing or breathing, is an emergency.
Do not place aspirin or heat on a painful tooth or gum.
proTips: Add a tooth-preservation kit and dental wax to your family first aid kit.
Use a mouthguard for contact sports and rough work.
Small cartons of shelf-stable milk can double as tooth storage in a kit.
Note the time the tooth came out - dentists use it to plan treatment.
source: American Association of Endodontists / Indian Health Service

sources.title: Knocked Out Teeth
First Aid for Dental Emergencies

whenNotTo: Do not replant a tooth in someone who is drowsy, confused, or seizing - they could inhale it.
Do not try to drain or lance a tooth abscess yourself.

quickGlance.situation: A tooth was knocked out or broken, or someone has a painful, swollen tooth or gum.
immediate: Pick up a knocked-out adult tooth by the crown; rinse with water only
Replant it and hold it, or keep it in milk or a tooth kit
Get to a dentist within 30 minutes
then: Broken tooth: rinse, cold compress, save pieces, see a dentist
Swelling to eye or neck, or trouble swallowing or breathing: emergency care
